Oṃ! Salutation to the one whose supreme reality is the body of the conscious self.
Now begins the *Paramārthasāra*, composed by the venerable Abhinavaguptācārya, the most excellent teacher of the Great Maheśvara.
Accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Yogarāja:
Victorious is the unborn Supreme Lord, who, though consisting of pure consciousness, has solidified into the form of the universe;
He is the masterful artist in the playful sport of concealing His own nature. (1)
I shall compose a brief commentary on this summary of the essence of the ultimate truth, which has been composed by my Guru through skillful means.
In this [work], the sacrifice requested by learned men has been performed. || 2 ||
In this teaching of non-dual Śiva, [the first yoga is that which consists in the predominance of the subjectivity of the body and so forth.
[Yoga, the teacher named Yogarāja.
Page 2.

Considering the completion of the treatise to be preceded by the total destruction of the flood of obstacles— consisting of doubt, fear, lethargy, and uncertainty arising from one's own mental constructs— he [proceeds] by casting aside the limited state of being a cognizer, [becoming] a single mass of consciousness and bliss.

First of all, she contemplates that supreme devotion to the Supreme Lord, which is characterized by immersion into one's own self as the deity, which contains the condensed essence of the meaning of all scriptures,
and which is beyond the beginning, profound, and situated in the Transcendent.
I take refuge in you alone, Śambhu— the one who is established as manifold within the caves [of the heart], the abode of all, and who dwells within everything moving and unmoving. || 1 ||

I take refuge in You— Śambhu, whose essence is the highest bliss, whose nature is pure existence, who is the very form of the deity that is one's own Self, and who is the quintessence of the radiance of all subjects—
as my protector for the sake of attaining complete immersion in You. The word "eva" (only) [emphasizes] Śambhu.

"I take refuge in the form of my own self as the deity alone, and not in some other separate deity who wanders within *māyā*"; thus, he excludes the possibility of any other connection. Furthermore, what is that [deity] like? It is supreme (*para*), complete (*pūrṇa*), consisting of consciousness, bliss, and will.

The supreme nature is replete with the powers of knowledge and action; likewise, it is "situated beyond the deep," meaning that from the reality called Māyā, which is the "deep," it exists as the other— the truly full.

He abides in his own essential nature within the pure path (śuddhādhvan), which extends from Śiva down to the principle of Vidyā; he does not, however, manifest even through the diversity of those various states. Consequently, there occurs for him a falling away from that supreme, full essential nature. As it has been said:

"Even though it expands through the various states such as waking and so forth, it does not deviate from its own essential nature as the perceiver, which remains undivided [from it]. Thus it is stated in the *Spanda-kārikā* (1.3). It is beginningless, ancient, and exists as the experiencer of all perceptions.

Because it is established from the beginning as the subject (*pramātṛ*), it is "one," meaning without companion, since differentiation is untenable due to its manifestation as the unity of consciousness (*cidaikya*). Likewise, regarding the phrase "established therein" and so forth: even that which is of such a nature, by its own sovereignty, manifests in many ways through various kinds of distinctions within the "caves"—that is, within the caves of the heart in the form of the Rudras and the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*).
Pervading within, although his own nature is consciousness, he manifests himself as both the insentient and the sentient, like an actor appearing in various roles as diverse subjects—
[namely: the Rudras, the lords of the worlds, the individual souls (kṣetrajñas), and the bound subjects (paśu-pramātāraḥ).

"— is situated"— this is the meaning. For this very reason, it is called "the abode of all" (*sarvālayam*), meaning the abode or place of rest for the entire universe consisting of subjects and objects, such as Rudra, the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*), and so forth.

Indeed, all this, while existing within the full subject (*pūrṇapramātṛ*), is designated by various forms as if it were emerging through differentiation and appearing with distinction in relation to the pair of grasped and grasper; otherwise, if it were separate from this Light, its very existence would not even be possible—how then could this universe exist? Thus it is said.
This is a reflection upon all pronouns.

He says "abiding in all that is moving and unmoving" to show that the Lord's true nature is not exhausted by this much alone— that is, He abides as the very form of this entire universe, which consists of both the insentient and the sentient.
"O All-pervading Lord, since You Yourself are indeed the creator of everything, therefore all this is You alone.
For, according to this principle, it is logically untenable for anything else that is distinct [from the Self] and unmanifest to be an effect.
"The enjoyer alone exists everywhere at all times in the form of the object of enjoyment" (Sp.
Thus, it is the Blessed Lord himself who shines forth in such and such ways—[I bow] to You, who are of this nature, the unsurpassed.

I take refuge in the Blessed Lord Śambhu, whose essential nature is the supreme non-dual light— an unbroken self-sovereignty that, while assuming manifoldness, is nonetheless the very core of the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*) which constitutes the true divine form of all things.

By means of the identification (*guṇīkāra*) of the artificial egoity consisting of the body and so forth with You alone—who are such a Self whose nature is the wonder of supreme subjectivity (*parāhantācamatkāra*)—I enter into [You]; this is the meaning. By this introductory formula, [the author indicates] the state consisting of immersion in one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), which is the supreme object of attainment.

By the teacher instructing [the disciple], an introduction to the meaning of the entire treatise has been made by way of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, as will be explained hereafter. (1)
Having thus established the essential nature of non-duality through the medium of praise— which is the intended purport of this treatise—
the author now declares the introduction of the scripture and states its relationship, subject matter, and so forth,
in two Āryā verses:
Wandering through the wheel of suffering from conception until death.
The disciple asked the Blessed One, the Supporter, about the ultimate truth.
Abhinavagupta explains that essence which the Guru spoke by means of the Ādhārakārikās.
By means of the yoga of the vision of the Śiva-scripture (6). (A pair of verses:

A certain person, having developed dispassion toward the cycle of existence through the grace of the Lord, with his mind turned away from worldly life, thinking "I am to be instructed by the Guru," [approached] the true Guru, the support, known as Śeṣa.

Having properly propitiated the Sage, he asked about the nature of the instruction on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Then, having considered that disciple’s inner mind to have been dissolved through the process of cultivating his own readiness and spiritual maturity, Anantanātha— who was himself a knower of the instructions of all the scriptures— [proceeded].

By means of this treatise titled *Paramārthasāra*, also known by the alternative name *Ādhārakārikā*—in accordance with the instructions set forth in the Sāṃkhya system—through the knowledge of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*... [page 7] ... [omitted].

"Attainment of the Supreme Brahman"— thus he spoke to this disciple. Considering that this very instruction on Brahman becomes logically consistent only when presented from the perspective of one's own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), which is the nature of supreme non-duality (*paramādvaya*), the Guru [proceeded] to grace all people by means of the reasoning of the supreme non-dual Śaiva system.
"Concealed" means hidden by a fresh, extraordinary expansion of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), thus being secret and accompanied by its esoteric mystery.

This very [work], which is a sequence of meritorious syllables, conveys its essence—that which is the essence of that instruction on the ultimate reality—as something to be accepted like butter from curd; for he is intent upon bestowing grace upon others.

Thus, the relationship, the subject matter, the title, and the purpose have been established; they will not be elaborated upon here again for fear of making this treatise too voluminous. What kind of disciple is he? To this he says: "concerning the dwelling in the womb.
[The soul] is born, exists, grows, transforms, and declines, beginning from the commencement of the dwelling in the womb.
"It perishes"— thus, through the variety of its various states,
it is joined to the wheel of the six transformations of existence, which consists of suffering ending only in death.

Because it has the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) through its appearance and disappearance, he is "whirling like a wheel" (*cakra*) within that [cycle], revolving about it. By this, his manifestation of awakening (*bodha*), which has the nature of recollecting his previous births, is illuminated;
otherwise, how could there be such curiosity regarding the question characterized by reaching the ultimate limit?
And thus, he who has attained detachment, whose heart has been pierced by the power of the Supreme Lord’s grace,

in whom right knowledge has arisen, and having become a fit vessel for instruction, having approached a suitable Guru who embodies the form of the Supreme Lord, and who desires the supreme non-dual knowledge— he alone [is such].
"One should become a vessel for the teacher's instruction"— this very point has been stated elsewhere:
"O Goddess, by the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), one is led toward a true guru."
"The supreme knowledge is bestowed, and the latent impressions of karma are destroyed"—thus it is said; and this will also be explained further on below. || 3 ||
[The three transformations themselves are the rim, the circumference of the wheel.

Now, having established the introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*) by way of the order of origination (*samutpattikrama*), within the variegated painting of the manifold diversity of the universe...

In this world, the single, unsurpassed sovereignty of the Supreme Lord alone is the cause of the power to join and disjoin; thus, demonstrating that the universe is merely the unfolding of His power through the fourfold cosmic egg (*aṇḍacatuṣṭaya*),
he introduces the treatise.
By the weight of the majesty of her own power, she [divides] these four cosmic eggs through differentiation;
that power is Māyā, Prakṛti.
And "the earth" was thus proclaimed by the Lord.

By the Lord, the independent and blessed Maheśvara, who is a single mass of consciousness and bliss, this fourfold egg has been formed as a solid mass of substance, existing in the form of a sheath that envelops the universe.
As it has been said:
"A mass of objects is called an egg (aṇḍa).
Thus it is manifested or revealed, or employed as the agent of becoming. Why? He says: "Because of the weight of the majesty of his own power."

Thus: from that abundance— that is, the fullness or intense overflow— of the majesty, which is the manifold expansion, of that collection of powers such as will (*icchā*) and the rest, which are innate, belonging to one’s own self, and unique.

It is said that the creation of the universe is indeed the expansion of the unfolding of the Blessed One’s own power (*śakti*). As it is stated in the venerable *Sarvamaṅgalā-śāstra*: "Power and the possessor of power—these two alone are said to be the categories of reality."
The entire universe is his power, while Maheśvara is the possessor of that power.

Thus [it is asked]: what is the nature of the number of the four eggs? He says: Śakti, Māyā, Prakṛti, and Pṛthvī. That which belongs to the Supreme Lord is the activity of negation consisting of the concealment (*apohana*) of one's own true nature—the state of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*)—even though the universe, which consists of subject and object, has as its essence the wonder of the supreme "I-consciousness" (*parāhantā*).
That very power, by virtue of its nature as a concealer and a binder, is called the *śaktyaṇḍa* (the egg of power);
it has petals extending as far as the principles (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā.
[Page 11]

This power, by way of being a sheath (*kośa*), remains having internally and completely encompassed the three eggs (*aṇḍa*) that are about to be described; it is designated by this term. Within this egg, Sadāśiva and Īśvara alone are the presiding lords.
Furthermore, that which consists of the nature of the three impurities (*mala*), is composed of delusion (*moha*), and— due to its exclusive inclination toward differentiation—

constitutes the bondage for all subjects, extending as far as the *puṃs-tattva* as its petals, is called the "egg" (*maṇḍa*) known as Māyā. And that [egg] stands having completely encompassed within itself the two eggs to be described hereafter.
And here, the Lord of the Egg (Aṇḍādhipati) is the Rudra named Gahana.

Likewise, Prakṛti—composed of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—having evolved in the form of both the object and the instrument of experience, exists as the object of enjoyment for the bound subjects (paśu-pramātṛs); she binds them by means of the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

The term "egg" (aṇḍa) refers to the designation of primordial nature (prakṛti). Within that as well, the Lord Viṣṇu, possessed of great majesty, is the sovereign of the egg, characterized by differentiation.
Likewise is the earth, and so on for all beings down to humans and stationary objects.
Because it exists as the form of each respective mode for cognizers (*pramātṛ*), consisting of a gross sheath (*kañcuka*) that binds them,
it is called the "Cosmic Egg of Earth" (*pṛthvyaṇḍa*). Furthermore, within that fourteen-fold creation of elements (*bhūtasarga*), it is the primary one.
"The Lord Brahmā is the sovereign of the egg"—thus this fourfold egg, which is the manifestation of the Supreme Lord, shines forth as revealed by the Blessed One in this manner. 4.

Having thus established these four eggs, he now states a *kārikā* to define the nature of the universe, with the intent of demonstrating the relationship between the object of experience and the experiencer within this very context:
"In that [egg], this entire universe exists within."
The continuous succession of diverse bodies, instruments, and worlds—
therein the embodied soul is the enjoyer, who is Śiva himself having assumed the state of a bound beast (paśu). || 5 ||
As it has been said:

"Taking up the egg of power as a lump of clay, the Blessed One repeatedly fashions the vessel of the cosmic egg by means of the staff of the root-egg, through the process of the revolving wheel of the egg of illusion."
The potter.
Thus: "The root" means primordial nature (*prakṛti*); "the root-egg" (*mūlāṇḍa*) means the egg of primordial nature.
In those four eggs well-known from the scriptures, this entire universe is contained within their midst.

It exists. Of what kind? He says: "Variegated" (*vicitra*). Bodies—meaning forms—which are distinguished by the difference between Rudras and individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), consisting of various arrangements of faces, hands, feet, and so forth, are wonderful in their nature as specific configurations. Likewise, they are characterized by excellence through their mutual differentiation.

The instruments are the eyes and so forth. For example, for subjects such as Rudra, these are unsurpassed and endowed with a multitude of qualities such as omniscience; by means of them, indeed, all this is known and accomplished simultaneously in a single moment. For the *kṣetrajñas*, however, these very same things are the instruments.

Governed by the power of destiny (niyati-śakti) of the Supreme Lord, these instruments are capable only of producing knowledge of specific objects such as a jar; they do not know everything, nor can they perform all actions. Even in that regard, there is a preeminent excellence of the instruments belonging to yogis—namely:

By transcending the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), even that which is distant, obstructed, or remote is discerned through his own instruments, as are the pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in another subject.

It is known that even among animals, although their senses are contracted by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), there exists a superiority over humans. For example: cows see their own home even when it is obstructed;
horses perceive the path even at night; vultures...

They perceive food even at a distance of a hundred yojanas; birds, from bees down to gnats, are seen dwelling in the sky; reptiles travel along paths on their bellies; they hear sounds with their eyes; and camels draw out a snake from a distant pit by its mere breath.

Thus, in this manner, the diversity of the instruments (karaṇa) is to be inferred everywhere. Likewise, the worlds (bhuvana), as established by the scriptures, possess extraordinary configurations in the form of circles, triangles, squares, half-moons, and umbrellas.
In this way, the nature of these bodies, instruments, and worlds is diverse, consisting of various excellences and wonders.

The continuum (*saṃtāna*) is the uninterrupted flow of bondage; that universe (*viśva*) which possesses such a nature is "this kind of universe. And within this universe, which is of such a nature and consists of the essence of the object of experience (*bhogya*), [the following occurs]—page 15—[omitted].

"One must become an enjoyer"—thus he says: "And the enjoyer therein is the embodied one. That individual soul (*aṇu*) who possesses a body defiled by the three impurities (*malas*) has a body that serves as the locus of experience; he is the embodied one, whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Within this [world] composed of pleasure, pain, and so forth, he is the enjoyer—the experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth—the limited subject (*paśupramātā*).

It is said: "Indeed, from the perspective of another subject, not even an atom's worth of difference exists; how then could there be such a wretched thing as a 'possessor of a body' distinct from that? As it has been stated:
'Even a single location of Brahman possesses the nature of all forms.'"
And it is both unsurpassable and non-conceptual.
Thus,
even within each single principle (tattva), there is the nature of all thirty-six principles.

And according to this principle, the Supreme Lord alone— the Great Light whose very nature is consciousness— endowed with His own power, appears as the subject entirely non-different from everything. Therefore, even if one were to admit the existence of an embodied being distinct from Him, its manifestation would be logically untenable, as it would not be manifest.

Existence is not determined. If it does manifest, then within that nature of the Supreme Brahman, there is but one cognizer who is non-different from manifestation itself; thus, with what further purpose would this [text] be concerned?

Establishing that difference consists in the nature of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, he says: "Śiva himself has assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu). This very Lord Śiva—who was just described as a single mass of consciousness and bliss, whose essential nature is absolute freedom (svātantrya)—is [the one] whose true reality is concealed by the hiding of his own nature.

Being in truth [Śiva], by his own will, having assumed— as if an actor— the role of the embodied subject, and being characterized by the state of a bound soul (paśu) because he is to be protected and is a creature, he is called the "embodied enjoyer" (dehī) in relation to this object of enjoyment composed of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which he has fashioned for himself; however, there is no category of entity whatsoever that exists apart from Śiva.

It exists. And it is this very Lord Śiva who, by his absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), brings forth as if in play the dyad of subject and object characterized as the enjoyer and the enjoyed, in relation to which this worldly transaction dominated by duality occurs. Therefore, this alone—

The sovereignty of the Supreme Lord is unsurpassed, such that even when He has assumed the state of a bound soul (*paśu*), characterized by the nature of enjoyer and enjoyed through the abandonment of His full essential nature, He remains so for all subjects (*pramātṛ*).
Shining forth within Himself as the experiencer, He is indeed Śiva, a single mass of consciousness and bliss. || 5 ||

Even so, if the cognizer is a single conscious nature (*citsvabhāva*), yet becomes manifold due to the diversity of subjects and objects beginning with *māyā*, how can it be designated as one despite this contradiction? And if it is one, why does it appear in manifold forms? It is like shadow and light.
Due to contradiction, the superimposition of contradictory properties follows; however, a single entity cannot be of multiple forms. As it has been said:
"This alone is the distinction and the cause of distinction among entities, namely, that they possess contradictory properties."
"Superimposition (adhyāsa) or a distinction of causes.
Thus, demonstrating a worldly example here, he supports the objection regarding the subject of the analogy.
Just as a pure crystal assumes the forms of various colors,
[so does the Self assume the forms of] gods, humans, animals, and trees—
Likewise, the Lord is also [the locus of] the nature of form.

Just as a single crystal gem, by assuming within itself the various diversities of thousands of limiting adjuncts such as lac-dye, blue, and so forth, becomes variegated in that way, yet its crystal-nature does not suffer any loss thereby; this indeed is the "gem-ness" of the crystal gem, namely—

Even when that [crystal] is colored by various particularities, there is for everyone at all times an uncontradicted cognition that "this is a crystal-gem. Only this much is conventionally expressed here: "these [colors], such as lac, are manifesting"—but the adjuncts such as lac do not qualify it as a cloth does, whereby its own essential nature would be lost.

It may be so. Therefore, this very purity of the jewel consists in the fact that it assumes forms that are of the nature of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), while simultaneously manifesting as its own essential nature. In the same way, this Lord (*īśvara*), though independent, a single mass of consciousness, and solitary—[page 19]—is likewise [pure].

In the mirror of its own self, which is perfectly clear, it maintains—as non-different from itself—the state of being the forms of all particularities, from gods and humans down to animals, birds, and immobile beings, as well as categories such as Rudras and individual souls (*kṣetrajñas*), which it has itself created;
and it does so with a variety of colors, like a crystal gem. Furthermore, from that [mirror]...

Because he has transcended [all limitations], he reflects upon his own Self— which, though appearing in manifold forms, is one— strengthened by this very unbroken wonder of "I. Even in this way, for him, there exists no spatial or temporal dimension whatsoever that is differentiated and capable of fragmenting his unity, in relation to which [he might be defined].
One might indeed raise objections against our Great Lord (Maheśvara), such as the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and so forth;

however, even by others, a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) characterized by direct perception—which, though permeated by various distinctions—is accepted as being one and the same. As it has been said:
In a variegated cognition, the blue and other [colors] are adjuncts of the cognition and do not exist apart from it;
for one who attempts to discern them as separate falls into an impossibility.

Thus it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika*. Furthermore, for the Knower who is complete in every respect, whose sole body is consciousness (*cidekavapuṣ*), and who is autonomous—how could those two, space and time, which are considered to be causes of differentiation by means of the diversity of forms and the diversity of actions, and which exist as his manifestors, [be such]? How [could they exist]?

These two alone would be the delimiters of that Blessed One. If indeed there were at some time a state of spatial and temporal separation from consciousness, then even that [separation] would result in the superimposition of contradictory attributes.

In that case, one might entertain the possibility that [the world] arose [from them]; however, since the establishment of their own existence is achieved solely through the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*), the Great Lord alone—though possessing manifold natures—is established as the one whose form is consciousness (*cinmūrti*). Furthermore, regarding the principle of difference (*bhedadharma*), the imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) would be utterly impossible. Thus, [verse 6].

Now, if it is argued that the cognizer, whose true nature is consciousness alone, is accepted as being one, yet becomes manifold upon assuming the state of body, organs, and the world—then, upon the destruction of the body and so forth, he himself would be destroyed; or, upon their production, he himself would be produced at that time. Thus, he would be [identical] for every individual cognizer.
It is differentiated by way of the six transformations of existence, such as "is born," "exists," and so forth;

and since the experience of heaven, hell, and so on is obtained for this very Blessed One through the variety of karma consisting of merit and demerit, how can it be said: "He is Śiva in his own essential nature"?
This is also established by means of an illustration:
"It moves, it moves, like water."
Just as the reflection of the moon remains steady when [the water] is still,
so too does this Great Lord, the Self, remain steady within the group consisting of the body, the organs, and the world.

Just as when a stream of water flows, the orb of the moon— the lunar form— which in reality remains in the sky and is inherently immobile, appears to go or move even though it has fallen into the current;
likewise, at that very same moment, when another body of water becomes still, that very same [moon]...
"The orb of the moon seems to undergo a change in its state"—thus is this imagined in both ways by all perceivers;

however, it is not actually so in the ultimate sense. Furthermore, the space and time residing in the water do not function as differentiators of the moon's own nature as it is perceived in the sky; they are merely...
The water itself is of such a nature; yet,
there is a conventional distinction made regarding the reflection of the lunar disc within it, based on whether that reflection appears to move or not, or whether it faces this way or that.

Thus, by this much, there is no impairment whatsoever to the true nature of the moon whether it is reflected in the waters of the Gaṅgā or fallen into mud; in the very same way, this Self, whose essential nature is consciousness, remains unchanged whether the aggregate of bodies, organs, and worlds created by itself has perished or has arisen.

And as for the notion that [the self] has arisen—this is merely a conventional expression for those deluded by illusion, like the moon reflected in water; it is not, however, that one's own self is born or dies. Thus it is said in the Gītā:
"It is never born, nor does it ever die."
This has not come into being, nor will it ever cease to be again; unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (2.20)
Thus, this Self is the Great Lord, independent, whose essential nature is the reflective awareness of His own entire self; He manifests as the experiencer of all subjects, and therefore,
when those various states are dissolved away, [He remains].

Or rather, [it exists] within its own essential nature even during manifestation. And this very thing constitutes the sovereignty of the Great Lord (*maheśānatva*) of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), namely that even while being the enjoyer of experiences such as heaven and hell through the state of a bound subject (*paśupramātṛtā*), [it remains so].

By virtue of being the experiencer of all, he is indeed the very nature of consciousness. On the contrary, if this state of the bound soul (paśu)— consisting of merit, demerit, heaven, hell, hunger, thirst, and so forth— which is determined as a bondage, were illuminated and grasped by the Lord through the light of His own Self, [then it would no longer be bondage].

Then it attains existence within itself as previously described; otherwise, being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how could it be said that this very Maheśvara is subject to the destruction of his own essential form? Only an object that is entirely constructed—such as the body and so forth—can be either produced or withdrawn, but not [the Self].

If the eternal Lord Consciousness were subject to occasional arising and destruction, then there would follow the consequence that the Self is manifold by virtue of being both the grasped and the grasper; therefore, the Self is indeed one, yet, existing with a nature of diverse forms as the grasped and the grasper,
it manifests once again as the single unity of all through its status as the experiencer of everything.
There is no impairment whatsoever of the doctrine of non-duality. || 7 ||

If it has been established through both reasoning and scripture that this Self of all is thus of the very nature of the universal manifestation (*viśvaprapañca*), whose ultimate reality is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), and who is the light of all because consciousness pervades everything— then why is it not recognized as one's own Self even in a clod of earth and the like, since there is no distinction?

That [distinction] is not perceived; or, even if it were admitted, this appearing distinction between the insentient and the sentient would not be consistent, and since worldly transaction consists of the forms of the insentient and the sentient—how could this be? To this, he says:
"Just as Rāhu, though invisible..."
In the same way,
although this Self is omnipresent,
it shines forth by taking on objects within the mirror of the intellect.

Although Rāhu wanders everywhere throughout the expanse of space, he is not perceived; yet, when there is an eclipse of a planet, he is observed as being present within the lunar form, manifesting [there], and is identified as "this is Rāhu."

Just as [the sun], though situated on the wheel of the stars, appears as if not situated there, so too here, although this Self exists as the innermost of all and is directly perceived through its very nature as one's own experience,
it is not perceived as such by everyone. However, when [the state of] the subjects consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka*...

In the mirror of the intellect, the reflecting surface of intuition, at the time of determining the objects of perception—namely, when accepting objects such as sound and so forth—it becomes the object of the "I-consciousness" in the form "I hear. At that time, by virtue of its nature as the perceiver, even while abiding in a clod of earth or similar objects, it remains clearly manifest; therein, one's own self shines forth for all.

He is perceived as having the singular form of one’s own direct experience; yet, because objects such as clods of earth consist of absolute darkness, he appears there as if non-existent even while present, just as Rāhu does in the sky. In this same way, by means of his power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), this Lord [appears] within the multitude of entities—which, though identical with his own self—consisting of some that take the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
It renders even objective fragments— which have been consecrated by the essence of the state of "I-ness"—
into subjects; it renders some into objects, in relation to which this [subject] exists.

The conventional distinction between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*), which consists in their respective natures, is indeed well-established. By that [distinction], a clod of earth and the like are insentient because they are objects of cognition (*vedyatva*), whereas the subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka* is sentient because it is the cognizer (*vedakatva*). However, this distinction between the insentient and the sentient does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) with respect to the Supreme Lord. — Thus [ends verse] 8.

Now, if the self indeed manifests without distinction within the intellect of all cognizers, then why would they all not be knowers of their own self? Whether they possess that knowledge or not, there is no difference [between them]. As for the fact that even during the state of transmigratory existence, some...
Through the knowledge of their own Self, some are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), endowed with omniscience and omnipotence;

some are seen to be fit for the knowledge of their own Self and have ascended [the path]; others, being devoid of the knowledge of their own Self, are transmigrating beings bound by the continuous fetters of auspicious and inauspicious karma caused by merit and demerit.
Thus, how is this consistent?
— [The answer is:
In this way, having performed everything internally, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) belonging to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*) is unshackled (*viśṛṅkhala*). Thus.
Just as a face shines forth in a mirror free from impurity, so does this [self] appear.
In the principle of consciousness, purified by the descent of Śiva’s power, there shines the nature of light.

Just as a face shines in a mirror free from impurity, endowed with its full range of qualities such as form and so forth without distinction— there is no place that a mirror whose stains have been removed does not accept— the face, however, in a stained mirror, though it possesses no inferiority, appears in a distorted manner due to its own turbidity. Nor...
A person who is impure is unable to adopt another's virtues; on the contrary, with his face turned away from them,
he perceives that very face as being otherwise— possessed of darkness and the like— and brings shame upon himself for his own deformity.

"Regarding 'my own face': in the very same way, that power of Śiva, one's own Self, which is called *anugraha* (grace), its descent is the expansion of its own rays; by means of that, when the mirror of intuition (*pratibhā*) has been cleansed, [the *āṇava*...]"

Due to the exhaustion of the latent impressions of the impurities of *māyā* and *karman*, [the Self] becomes clarified; for certain knowers (*pramātṛs*) who are in their final birth, it is "consisting of light" (*bhārūpa*), meaning its form is light— thus, even as far as it is endowed with the multitude of qualities such as omniscience and so forth, it manifests as such.

Because their own essential nature is manifest, those [beings] are, for all intents and purposes, liberated and possess excellence, even though they have fallen into the midst of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). For some, however, because the *buddhi*-principle is completely veiled by the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* through the power of the Supreme Lord’s concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*), the Self— though consisting of light— is perceived as if stained, despite being luminous.

He is as if non-existent, by which those transmigratory beings are designated as "animals"; yet others, due to their connection with both powers, are "aspirants" (*ārurukṣu*). Thus, there is a variety of descents of power (*śaktipāta*) according to the distinctions of intense, mild, very mild, and so forth.

This should be applied everywhere. Herein, no action whatsoever— whether it be the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and so forth, or recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and the like— arising from the power of necessity (*niyatiśakti*) which falls within the realm of illusion (*māyā*), is the cause of liberation for the self.
For, because he has transcended *māyā*, an object characterized by duality is not suitable for the means of attaining him. As it is sung:
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen [in this way]" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.53).
Thus, for those of auspicious intellect, the sole cause here is the unartificial grace of the Supreme Lord. As it has been said:
"In the portion consisting of the descent of the Lord's power, [the scripture] makes manifest His sovereignty."
The intellect, when perfumed by the causal power, does not depend on anything at all.

Thus it is said. For limited subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*), however, the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) belonging to the Supreme Lord is precisely the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

By means of this, because their own true nature does not manifest, they remain intent upon auspicious and inauspicious karma, partaking in the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and thus transmigrate again and again in this world. Therefore...

Even though the self is common to all subjects, there are indeed two powers within it—those of grace (*anugraha*) and concealment (*tirodhāna*), which consist respectively of manifestation and non-manifestation; these two are the causes for the distinction between liberation and bondage. As it has been said:
(According to the venerable Avadhūtasiddhapāda:
"A certain power of the one of infinite power binds the knower of the field with unimpeded nets of worldly existence."
And having severed all qualities without exception with the sword of knowledge,
it brings the Puruṣa face-to-face with liberation.
Thus [ends the ninth].
Having thus established that all this is consistent with scripture, experience, and reasoning, [the author states:

that which was previously described as the fourfold egg (*aṇḍa*) beginning with *Śakti*— the universe consisting of thirty-six principles (*tattva*) existing within its interval, which shines forth as it is supported by that [foundation]— is, first of all, the cause of causes.
He describes the nature of Paramaśiva with two verses:
"He is of the nature of light, perfectly full, and great bliss due to resting within His own self."
It is filled with the instruments of will and consciousness, and is completely replete with infinite power.
Devoid of all conceptual constructions, pure, peaceful, and free from both dissolution and arising.
In that supreme reality,
the universe consisting of thirty-six principles shines forth.

The meaning is this: that supreme, perfect Śiva-tattva of such a nature—in which the entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth, as will be described hereafter, shines while resting and appearing as non-different from it—is established through reasoning. Now, [it may be asked: "But everything, beginning with the body (tanu), is expanded [from it]."

"In that [reality] there is *tattva*; or, because it extends (*tanana*) until the dissolution of the world (*āpralaya*), its state is *tattva*—thus, even if this designation of *tattva* were to somehow imply insentience (*jāḍya*) regarding the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva, who is of the nature of consciousness, it is replied: from the perspective of those to be instructed, it is designated by whatever word is used to convey it."
To that extent, there is a designation of "reality" (tattva) there, but not in an ultimate sense. What is that supreme reality like?
It is that whose light (*bhās*)—meaning its manifestation, form, and intrinsic nature—is great illumination; that is to say, its very body is great light. And likewise— [page 32] —

It is complete and free from desire. Yet, even that which is free from desire—such as insentient objects like crystal gems and mirrors—is not [the ultimate state]; thus he says: "Great bliss through resting in one's own self. Through resting in one's own nature, within the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the wonder of indivisible I-consciousness (*ahantā*), there arises great bliss, the supreme [bliss].

"Of which there is cessation" (nirvṛtiḥ yasya). Thus, because its essence consists of the radiance of supreme bliss, the distinction from insentient objects such as crystal—which are merely to be illuminated—is stated. For this very reason, he says:
"filled with the instruments of will and consciousness. It is indeed of the nature of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
Furthermore, it is not devoid of power and insentient like those who proclaim a quiescent Brahman;

rather, it is "filled with infinite powers. Infinite means innumerable; the powers consisting of names and forms, such as pots, cloths, and so forth, are the offshoots of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.

The powers beginning with Brahmyā arise from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*); by them, [the Lord] is completely filled and pervaded on all sides. Therefore, they shine forth from that very source and subside back into that same place.
In this way, the Lord’s sovereignty, whose nature is the supreme word (*parāvāk*), has been described. Now, if it is the case that the supreme [reality] is of the nature of speech...
In that case, reality is conceptual because it is permeated by words; how, then, can it exist within the essence of pure luminosity?

With the intention of asking, "What is the application of conceptual construction? he says: "devoid of all conceptual construction. That wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*) which exists in the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), although consisting of speech, is free from conceptual construction. For conceptual construction, characterized by the exclusion of the other (*anyāpoha*), implies a duality in the form of "pot" and "non-pot," thereby delimiting [the pot] as distinct from what is not a pot.

One determines "the jar. However, for Light—which has as its essence the wonder of supreme I-consciousness—there exists no non-luminous entity other than Light itself that could stand as its opposite; for it is through the exclusion of such an entity that Light would assume the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Indeed, an object capable of being excluded must be non-luminous in nature, whereas [Light] is the very body of Light.
"If it manifests,
then [it does so] through the realization of identity with the nature of its own cognition" (Svacchanda Tantra 3.28)—
according to this principle, how could even that object which has attained the nature of manifestation [be otherwise]?
It would have to be a differentiator of that very self, by which it would bring about a state of conceptualization therein.
Or, if it does not manifest as its opposite—how [could this be]?
(page 34)

Could it even be possible to determine that "here there exists an unmanifest object which is the nature of the opposite"?—this would be a mere trifle. For the supreme reality is devoid of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consisting of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), and its nature is undifferentiated. Therefore, he says "pure" (*śuddha*).

It is *vimala* (stainless), because of the absence of the impurity consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Likewise, it is *śānta* (quiescent), because of the absence of agitation arising from the subject-object duality; it abides in its own essential nature through the state of equilibrium of power (*śakti-sāmarasya*), and is not like a mere fragment of stone. Furthermore, it is "devoid of dissolution and emergence" (*layodayavihīna*).

"Since this Self is once and for all manifest," it is eternal. Therefore, time—consisting of past, future, and present forms—does not apply to it, because time itself arises from that very source; thus, it is excluded from both origination and destruction.
It would have been demonstrated that once the Supreme Reality is accepted, the "universality" of the universe is logically established. || 11 ||

Now, as for what has been established—that the world appears within such a supreme reality (*paratattva*)—how can this be so? For, in relation to the supreme reality, nothing at all would be capable of appearing as distinct.
If the world appears as distinct from it, then the doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*) is undermined; if it is non-distinct, then [the world is simply] the world...

"How can there be the verbal expression 'it shines'?"— anticipating this, [the author] says "just as in the reflection in a mirror" in order to demonstrate, by means of an illustration, that reality consists of both difference and non-difference, and to establish this point.
The city, village, and so forth, though variegated and without division,
appear as if divided from one another, even as in a mirror.
Due to the awakening to the most stainless and supreme Bhairava, which is likewise devoid of division,
[the world] appears both mutually and even from that [awakening] itself.
This world appears as differentiated. || 13 ||
Just as within the interior of a stainless mirror, there appear all things— cities, villages, towns, walls, towers, grounds,
rivers, streams, fires, trees, mountains, beasts, birds, women, men, and so forth.

By way of being reflections, it appears as variegated and manifold in its specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*); yet, being undivided and non-distinct from the mirror, it shines while imparting its internal form precisely through that non-difference. In this regard, although it appears without distinction, it also appears as mutually distinct by way of their respective individual characteristics (*anyonya-svālakṣaṇyena*).

"A cloth is different from a jar; a jar is different from a cloth"—thus it appears as distinct. For it is indeed the objects contained within that are perceived as separate; however, nothing at all is apprehended apart from that mirror. Rather, although the world exists in a state of identity with the mirror, it appears as if entirely distinct from it.
It is perceived. Even so, one might object that the mirror would then be hidden by the reflection of the jar and other objects;
to this he says, "And even from the mirror. Not only do entities themselves appear as distinct when situated within the mirror, but they are also perceived as being separate from the mirror itself.
For a mirror, although it consists of various reflections, shines as having a nature transcending those reflections; it does not, however, become identical with them, whereby—

The cognition "this is a mirror" would arise; moreover, even when everyone perceives various reflections therein, the uncontradicted understanding remains that "this is a mirror. Nor does a jar or other object qualify the mirror such that there would be a loss of its own essential nature here, leading to notions like "this is a jar-mirror" or "this is a cloth-mirror."

Whether the distinction is made by place or by time, it does not lead to the destruction of the essential nature [of the mirror]. Therefore, while being capable of receiving various reflections, the mirror remains a mirror within itself; thus, there is no impairment whatsoever to the theory of reflection. Now, it might be argued that this notion—that "there is an elephant in this mirror"—is an illusion.
It is perceived, yet it does not exist at all in the mirror, because it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as such;
this determination arises solely through delusion (*bhrānti*). By this much, the illustration according to the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*) is established. As for delusion, however—
The essential nature [of consciousness] is now being defined immediately following this. In the same manner,
by means of the analogies of the reflection in a mirror, a city in the sky, and so forth, [it is shown to arise] from the most pure and supreme awakening of Bhairava.
From that Light— which is intensely free from temporal limitations and overflowing with full bliss— the entire universe,

though devoid of division and undivided from that Light, manifests in manifold forms through the distinction between subject and object, like reflections in a mirror, even while remaining non-different from it.

And even from that—meaning, even from consciousness—it appears as if emerged, because consciousness, while manifesting even in the form of that [object], shines forth as transcending it, just as a mirror [transcends] its reflections. Even so, the Light, which is capable of receiving the reflections of all objective existents, transcends all objective existents. Of everything...

It manifests in its own essential nature as the experiencer. Even though distinctions of space, time, and form pertain to objects, they manifest here merely like reflections in a mirror; they do not, however, fragment its own nature. For this very reason, consciousness, although possessing both a singular and manifold nature, is indeed one, just like the variegated cognition admitted by the Buddhists. However—

There is this much distinction between the light of consciousness— which possesses wonder through the illumination of a mirror— and [the mirror itself]: that in the mirror, there is merely the quality of transparency.
An external object such as a city, which is distinct [from consciousness], appears as if it were a reflection, yet it is not something created by itself;

therefore, the determination that "this is an elephant in the mirror" would be an error. Light (prakāśa), however, whose essence is its own wonder, by its own will, perceives [objects] non-differently upon the wall of its own self.

The universe manifests solely by taking its own self-awareness as its material cause; the Lord’s status as creator is nothing other than this manifestation of the universe. Thus, reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) alone is the primary form of Light, which establishes its distinction from inert reflections such as those in a mirror. This very point—
The author of the work has stated in the *Vivṛtivimarśinī*:
"Just as a world of diverse arrangements shines within a mirror, so does the entire universe shine here within the Self."
Furthermore, consciousness, by means of the principle whose essence is its own self-reflection, perceives the universe; a mirror, however, does not do so.

Thus, with respect to the Supreme Lord, there is no delusion of duality whatsoever regarding the multitude of entities fashioned from His own limbs; however, with respect to the subject under the influence of *māyā*, this appearance of duality which occurs— this [is what follows].
Error consists in the non-manifestation of fullness; that is, the non-appearance of the nature of the full, non-dual Self.
Fullness does not appear, but rather the incomplete, dual form appears; in other words, only difference is perceived. Therefore, this theory of reflection is faultless. || 13 ||

Thus, having first established the nature of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and the existence of the universe— consisting of thirty-six principles— as non-different from that Light, he further explains the essential nature of each individual principle according to the order of its emergence through these verses.
The state of the principles consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā,
along with that of the five Śaktis.
He illuminates by means of the state of being differentiated. || 14 ||

This very Paramaśiva, whose essential nature has just been explained by way of the form of the supreme reality (paratattva), possesses those powers (śaktis) whose nature is identical to his own essential nature.
The five [powers] known as will, satisfaction, knowledge, action, and [the fifth] are the causes of the multitude of infinite powers;
by means of the differentiation of these very five powers and through the exclusion of what is not that,
He manifests this state of reality (tattvadaśā) as delimited by the number five according to its own specific characteristics.

It reveals—this is the meaning. Of what sort is she? To this he says: "Śiva," and so forth. She is thus described as one whose nature (*bhāva*) consists of Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva; likewise, she is one in whom Īśvara and Vidya are the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*). Herein, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of each principle (*tattva*) [is to be understood].

It is demonstrated as follows: indeed, that consciousness which exists within all subjects—consisting of the wonder of the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness), transcending all categories (*tattva*), and having the nature of the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*)—is precisely the *Śivatattva*. Here, the definition of the categories is presented with respect to those who are to be instructed. Of that very Lord, whose form is consciousness...
Consisting of the nature of bliss, for one who reflects "I am the universe," consciousness itself— whose very essence is the state of being the universe— assumes a slight state of swelling.

This is the seed-ground of all existents; it is the state of potentiality (*śaktyavasthā*). Although it possesses both the forms of the "diminished" (*kṛśa*) and the "full" (*pūrṇa*) through the metaphorical application of universal emanation and reabsorption, it is celebrated as one alone in all the systems of secret doctrine. Furthermore, within this very ground, which is the seed of the universe’s emergence...

In that which is called the Great Void and the Supreme Void, there is the wonder consisting of the full *ahantā* (I-ness) of Maheśa as "I am this," due to non-differentiation; because of the predominance of knowledge (*jñāna*), the aspect of action (*kriyā*) rests within *ahantā*. This is the state of Sadāśiva. Here, the subjects are the Mantramaheśvaras.

They remain. Likewise, in this very state, that wonder of one's own Self (*svātmacamatkāra*)—in which "I" and "this" are held in equilibrium like the pans of a balanced scale through non-differentiation as "I am this"—is his state of Īśvara.
Here too, the Mantreśvaras are the subjects (*pramātāraḥ*). Here too, it is by virtue of the predominance of "this-ness" (*idantā*)...
That wonder which, through the attribution of the quality of "I-ness," takes the form of "I, I" and "this, this," like that of a newborn infant...

It is to be indicated by the head and the fingers; for this very reason, because it is the essence of awakening, it is the Bhagavat’s *śuddhavidyā-tattva*. Here, along with the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), there are seven groups of eight mantras which, by virtue of their nature as grace, act as the designators (*vācaka*) in order to elevate the bound souls (*paśu*s) who are the designated objects (*vācya*).

They abide in relation to the Mantramaheśvaras and Mantreśvaras. Here, within this Vidyātattva, although there is no difference in the fact that the subjects—the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara-pramātṛ)—are essentially of the nature of consciousness, the manifestation of duality that occurs is caused solely by the power of Māyā; so it is proclaimed in the Āgamas.
"Mahāmāyā above Māyā"—thus [it is said]. Because the mantras situated therein enter into Mahāmāyā, they are called *aṇavaḥ*.
Above the principle of Māyā and below Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) are the subjects who are the Vijñānākala-s.

The vessel for the *āṇava* impurity. Thus, this single nature of Śiva, although transcending the fourth state (*turyātīta*), is celebrated as having the form of the fourth (*turya*) and as the fivefold reality (*tattvapañcaka*). Therefore, this one independent agent alone shines forth; that light which exists on the plane of Sadāśiva and Īśvara as "I am this" is precisely this.

The instrument (*karaṇa*) consists of pure sensation and form; the effect (*kārya*) is the creation of the principles (*tattvasarga*), beginning with the principle of Māyā and ending with Earth, which will be described hereafter.
—In this way, the single supreme subject, known as the Great Lord of one's own self, manifests in the form of agent, instrument, and action. || 14 ||
He states the essential nature of the principle of Māyā:
it is that supreme sovereignty of the Great Lord which accomplishes the impossible.
The Goddess Māyā-śakti is this veil of Śiva’s own self. || 15 ||

That supreme, absolute sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, which is independent of anything else and constitutes His state as the creator of the universe— that very thing is this power called *māyā* belonging to that possessor of power (*śaktimān*). It is called *māyā* because by it the manifold expansion of subjects and objects, ending with the earth, is measured— that is, delimited.

Or, it is *māyā* because it deludes the universe. It is called *Devī* (the Goddess) because she belongs to the Lord who is by nature playful; however, no separate *māyā* arises as it does for the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*). What is that sovereignty like? It is "the accomplishment of the difficult-to-accomplish" (*durghaṭasaṃpādana*). That is, it is that which is to be brought about with difficulty.
It is possible—
page 45—
to accomplish a difficult task consisting of the nature of the cognizer and the cognized.

That which brings about attainment [is as follows]: this very Māyā is the triad of impurities—Āṇava and the rest—which constitutes the veil over one's own self and is termed the "concealment of one's true nature" for Śiva when he has assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu) by his own will. || 15 ||

And regarding the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) which will be described as consisting of pleasure and so forth, and which is divided according to its primary nature— [the author] states the essential nature of that *puṃstattva* (the principle of the person), which is the subject of enjoyment (*bhoktṛ*), [as being] due to the influence of the grasping of *māyā*.
The person whose consciousness is defiled becomes a bound soul (paśu);
bound by the power of time, the divisions of time, and necessity, and under the influence of passion and ignorance. 16.

Due to its dependence on the acceptance of *māyā*, consciousness—though consisting of omniscience and omnipotence—has fallen into the *āṇava* impurity, which is of the nature of non-recognition (*akhyāti*), by casting aside qualities such as omniscience; whereby...
[page 46]

When the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is by nature all-pervasive like the space within a jar, becomes delimited and restricted, that very state is called the principle of the individual soul (*puṃstattva*). Therefore, being the one to be protected and bound by *māyā*, he is the "bound soul" (*paśu*), the receptacle for the fetters (*pāśa*) whose natures are the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*. Furthermore:

The principle of the individual soul (puruṣatattva) is thus completely bound and woven together by Time and the other factors—whose natures will be described below as "parts of time" (kālakalā)—and is encircled by the six principles. || 13 ||
He now states the essential nature of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Time (kāla) according to this sequence of envelopment: "Right now, I know only this much, as the self of all."
This group of six coverings (kañcukas), together with Māyā, is said to be internal to the individual soul (aṇu). || 17 ||
Just as independent consciousness itself has attained a state of atomicity through its own *māyā*, so too have its powers of knowledge and action [attained such a state].

When this [consciousness] in the form of a bound soul (paśu) is contracted, it is said to possess the two powers known as *vidyā* and *kalā*. Just as a person whose entire wealth has been confiscated by a king might be given a small amount of money out of compassion for the sake of survival,
so too is [the power] given to consciousness that has attained the state of atomicity (*aṇutva*) and has had its omniscience and other qualities stripped away.

The state of being a knower (*jñatva*)—the ultimate reality of limited agency—is reinforced; thus, because of the primacy of the state of being a knower, the connection of time and the other [categories] with the verb "to know" is demonstrated. This group of six coverings (*kañcuka*), joined with the aforementioned form of *māyā*, belongs to the individual soul (*aṇu*), a person whose omniscience and other qualities have been cast aside by the *āṇava* impurity.
It is said to be an internal, innate [impurity] that obscures one's own true nature, like a tarnish on gold. Of what form is it?
To this he says "now," and so forth. "I know only now"—thus that limited soul (aṇu) perceives through the lens of the present tense:
"this was known by me previously, I know it now, and I shall know it"; likewise, "it was done thus, I am doing it," and so on.

Thinking "I shall do," while thus fashioning even entities through the nature of knowledge and action, he also delimits them—this is his "time. Likewise, by thinking "only this much," he makes that which is already delimited;
[the meaning is: having delimited himself, who stands as the eternal substratum, as past, future, and present.]

It is not capable of doing everything; it is able to produce only a jar, not a cloth or other things—this is the *kalā*-principle of this *aṇu*. This very principle is that from which a specific effect necessarily arises due to a specific cause.

It "demands" (arthayate) in this way: for instance, smoke arises from fire alone, and the fruit of heaven and so forth arises only from rituals such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), not from everything; that by which the self is thus constrained by the merit and demerit arising from a continuous stream of actions performed according to its own volition through such a restriction is its principle of necessity (niyatitattva).
Likewise, "with one's whole being" refers to this sense of incompleteness—the thought: "All this is useful to me;

may I exist more fully, and may I never cease to exist"—this is the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*) belonging to the bound soul (*paśu*). As for the passion that is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), it consists in excluding everything else and fixing upon some single object characterized by beauty, thinking: "My passion is directed toward this."

It is merely attachment, not identical to the essence of passion (*rāga*) which consists of all forms of longing. Likewise, it is "I know" something standing right before one, such as a jar, and not an object that is distant or concealed—this is the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*). In relation to pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) in the *Kārikā*, but not [in the sense of being a total lack of knowledge].
Because of the absence of [true] sensation; accompanied by illusion (māyā), it is joined with the manifestation of duality—this is the sixfold covering (kañcuka) of the bound soul (paśu). || 17 ||
How is it that this sixfold sheath is internal to the individual soul (aṇu)? To this he says: Like the husk situated within a grain of rice, it is distinct yet non-different.
That [mind], however, attains purity through the application of being oriented toward the auspicious path. || 18 ||

Just as a kernel of rice, though distinct by its actual nature, appears as non-different when placed within a grain of rice due to its lack of separation; and even when carefully extracted by experts,
it does not remain separate because of its intimate connection with the rice— so too [is the case here].

This sheath of *māyā* and the rest, although distinct from the individual soul (*aṇu*)—which is like the grain of rice—because it is internal, remains as if non-distinct, covering the nature of perfect consciousness, which is like the kernel; this is the implied meaning. Even so, how can that [sheath], which is difficult to remove, be dissolved?

Thus he says, "He partakes," and so forth. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction: there is no other means here. That which is the path of Śiva—the Great Lord of one’s own self—is this: "I am the single, dense mass of supreme non-dual consciousness and bliss."

The path that consists of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one's own essential nature as the manifestation of one's own power— namely, "this entire universe is mine alone"— and the firm orientation toward it, characterized by being intent upon its contemplation, is itself *yoga* in its full form within the limited individual (*aṇu*) in his own self.

The relationship [of the soul] is by virtue of its own essential nature (*svasvarūpatva*); therefore, that aforementioned covering (*kañcuka*), possessing such a nature, attains purification specifically and undergoes complete dissolution of its own accord. This is what is meant:
when the bound soul (*paśu*) becomes one whose heart is purified by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*parameśvara-śaktipāta*), then [he realizes], "I am indeed..."

"Maheśvara" [means that] through the manifestation of the knowledge of one's own self, the covering of the *kañcukas* which brings about the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) dissolves by itself; furthermore, in this state, apart from the knowledge of one's own self, no other power of *māyā*—such as action arising from the power of necessity (*niyati*)—prevails. || 18 ||
Thus, for such an atom (aṇu) and an enjoyer, there must be an object of enjoyment;
with this in mind, he describes the creation of the principles (tattva) belonging to primordial matter (pradhāna).
Consisting solely of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and arising from determination, conceptualization, and self-conceit,
Nature (prakṛti) is thus the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Intellect, mind, and ego-sense, in this order. || 19 ||

That which is the common form of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, wherein no relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is perceived—that is *prakṛti*, the root cause.
Immediately following *prakṛti*, he describes the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in its form as an effect, beginning with the word "ascertainment" (*niścaya*). Ascertainment...

The thought "this is such-and-such"—namely, conceptualization (*saṃkalpana*), reflection (*manana*), and the conceit of "mine" (*mamatā*)—is, in this sequence, the triad consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), the mind (*manas*), and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
This triad constitutes the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
it is the effect of the *guṇas* through their relationship as cause and effect, and it is the cause with respect to the elements, the senses, and so forth.
Thus [ends the section]. 19.
He states the external organs:
the ear, skin, eye, and tongue.
The nose and the other sense organs [are directed] toward sound and the rest;
furthermore, speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action. (20)

Regarding the objects to be described, such as sound and the rest, there are the five sense organs beginning with the ear, which have cognition as their primary function, and the five organs beginning with speech, which have action as their primary function. The objects of the organs of action consist of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure. Thus, they are of both kinds.
"I hear," "I speak"—these are the effects of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), because they follow from it. || 20 ||
He describes the nature of their objects, such as sound and so forth:
"The object to be grasped by these [senses] would be subtle and devoid of differentiation."
That [evolves into] the five subtle elements (tanmātra): sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. || 21 ||

That which is to be accepted as the object and sphere of these senses by virtue of being their knowable effect—what is it like? It is devoid of division; that is, specifically excluded from particulars, it is of the nature of the universal (sāmānya).

That object which is subtle is itself the generic form of sound and so forth; that is the "mere-tanmātra," namely, the generic sound, or *śabda-tanmātra*. The same applies to the others. Because the object and the subject are mutually dependent, this pentad of *tanmātras* is also purely derived from *ahaṅkāra*, just like the sense organs.
Because of the mutual intermingling of the objects of the senses, earth and the other elements constitute the effect; thus he says:
"By virtue of this combination, the gross object indeed attains the state of the five elements."
The wind, fire, water, and earth ascend into the sky. || 22 ||
Through the power of their conjunction and mutual friction,
that specific gross object itself attains the state of being the primary elements (*bhūta*).
To explain: from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), space (*nabhas*) arises as a specific quality of sound;

from sound and touch (*sparśa*), air (*pavana*); from these two joined with form (*rūpa*), fire (*tejas*); from these joined with taste (*rasa*), water (*āpaḥ*); and from these joined with smell (*gandha*), earth (*pṛthvī*)—thus arise the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūtāni*).

"Because they correspond to cause and effect, they possess qualities increasing by one. Thus, this primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of cause and effect, has proceeded as an object of enjoyment for the Supreme Lord, the Person (*puruṣa*), by His will.
Having thus divided the world consisting of thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), it has been described principle by principle. || 22 ||
Like a sheath of illusion, the creation preceded by *prakṛti* acts as a sheath for the *puruṣa*, just as husks cover a grain of rice.
This [universe], extending as far as the earth,
is consciousness appearing in the form of a body.
This primary creation, extending up to the level of the Unmanifest (Parā), is like the husk and the grain-skin that envelops a single grain of rice.

Just as it covers [the grain], in that very way, consciousness (caitanya), already enveloped by the shell-like garment of *māyā*, is again covered by this state of embodiment (*dehabhāva*) which stands in the place of the husk; it conceals it by acting as a surrounding wall. Herein lie these subjects (*pramātāraḥ*), [along with] the *kalās*.

All those whose nature is the body are said to be "sakala" (with parts), by virtue of possessing the sense organs (*indriya*) up to the specific objects (*viśeṣa*); and those devoid of specific objects are "videha" (bodiless) *pralayākala*s. Thus, the universe is presided over by the seven levels of subjects beginning with Śiva and ending with the *sakala*, and is governed by Rudra, Kṣetrajña, and Ādhiṣṭhita. || 23 ||
He describes the nature of the three sheaths as supreme, subtle, and gross:
"In this system, impurity (mala) is the supreme covering; the sheaths beginning with Māyā are the subtle; and [the remaining sheaths] are the gross."
The external form is the body;
indeed, the Self is enveloped by three sheaths.
The internal *āṇava* impurity is precisely *akhyāti* (non-apprehension), whose nature consists in the concealment of the true essence of consciousness,
just as tarnish is to gold.
The supreme internal obscuration is concealment (*chādana*), because it exists as one's very identity (*tādātmyena*).
The six coverings (*kañcuka*) beginning with *māyā* and ending with *vidyā* are the subtle obscuration of the Self;
like the husk of a grain of rice, they remain as an obscuration cast behind [the Self], by which [the state] consisting of duality arises.

The manifestation of [limited] subjectivity, agency, and so forth, which thus unfolds, is this impurity of *māyā*. In relation to this, the external, husk-like, and gross covering consisting of the existence of the body— characterized by the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and composed of skin, flesh, and so on— is the third, the impurity of action (*kārmamala*), by which the cognizer [is bound].

It becomes a vessel for the accumulation of auspicious and inauspicious karma. Thus, though it is expansive, the Self—being enveloped by these three sheaths consisting of the supreme, the subtle, and the gross—is contracted like the space within a jar; therefore it is called "atomic" (aṇu), a "bound soul" (paśu). || 24 ||
On account of this connection, he becomes as if impaired; thus it is said:
"Due to the conjunction with the darkness of ignorance, [one perceives] even one's own single nature, the Self..."
One should understand it through the manifold variety of the grasped and the grasper. || 25 ||
This Self, connected with the three sheaths, due to its connection with the darkness of the non-apprehension of the Self,
though it is one and of a non-dual nature, does not perceive itself as its own, innate [nature], nor as something other than that which has arisen from another.

Consciousness (*caitanya*), which is the self-nature (*ātmasvabhāva*) and the essential form (*svarūpa*) characterized by the existence of the Self, perceives through the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of the various arrangements of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*); that is to say, it conceives [itself] through duality (*bheda*), which is the opposite of non-duality (*abheda*).
This is just as a person afflicted by the visual impairment of *timira* perceives even a single moon [as many].
Seeing [two moons] and determining that "these two moons exist in the sky," he even shows it to others,
saying, "Look, these two moons!"— in reality, however, this moon is only one; yet, due to the influence of the cataract (*timira*),
it appears in such a way that the person with the cataract performs a causal function characterized either by agitation or by joy.

He attains [this state].— In the very same way, one who seeks the diversity produced by the cataract of ignorance (*ajñānatimira*), though everything is non-different from his own self, engages with it as if it were different and thus desires a differentiated fruit of action (*karmaphala*),
by which he becomes a partaker of the experiences of heaven, hell, and so forth, again and again. And therefore, because of the cataract of ignorance...
It is "form" (rūpa) because it appears in a distorted manner. || 25 ||
He demonstrates the non-duality of the self by means of an analogy:
[the stages of] juice, molasses, and sugar-candy.
Just as molasses, sugar-candy, and the like are nothing but sugarcane juice,
so too are all the various states of existence nothing but the Supreme Self, Śambhu. 26.

Just as various types of sugarcane, such as those with different tastes, are in reality nothing but a single sugarcane juice because sweetness permeates them all, so too are all the particular distinctions consisting of the manifold of subject and object— the various states such as waking and the rest— nothing but the Supreme Self, which is one's own true nature.

It belongs to Śambhu, the Great Lord of Consciousness alone. For that very Blessed One, being the self-nature of all, having entered into various states through his own sovereignty, manifests as characterized by the conditions of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth— just like sugarcane juice— and not otherwise.

Therefore, there exists nothing whatsoever distinct from one's own self; thus, he is indeed one alone, because consciousness persists through all states. In this way, by perceiving a single uniform nature everywhere, the cognizer becomes an all-seeing observer.
As the venerable Śambhubhaṭṭāraka has said:
A single entity has the nature of all entities;
all entities have the nature of the single entity.
He by whom one single entity is seen in its true nature has seen all entities in their true nature.
Thus it is said; and also in the Bhagavadgītā:
"Know that knowledge to be sattvic by which one perceives the one imperishable reality in all beings, undivided within the divided. (18.20)
Thus [ends the section]. 16.

However, the distinction postulated by other schools is accepted for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), but it is not tenable on the level of ultimate reality (*satya*); thus says the Inner Controller of Consciousness (*vijñānāntaryāmin*):
These range from the vital breath (prāṇa), the cosmic body (virāḍdeha), the genus (jāti), down to the individual body (piṇḍa);
this is merely conventional usage, for in the ultimate sense they do not exist at all. || 27 ||
"Consciousness" (vijñāna) is merely pure awareness, absolute and devoid of limiting adjuncts; although it is free from name and form,
by virtue of the power of the diversity of the awakening of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), [it appears as such].
The Vijñānavādins maintain that blue, pleasure, and so forth, which appear in various forms as external objects, are in reality [nothing but consciousness].
"All this is indeed the Self (Puruṣa)."

According to the principle, "There is no diversity whatsoever here," the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) maintain that the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) of all is the Supreme Brahman itself which, through the power of beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyā), manifests as differentiated. In both these cases, the autonomy of consciousness (vedanasya svātantryam) [is established].
It has not been considered that [the Self] is the life-force and the cause of the manifestation of the universe.

However, other proponents of *prāṇa-brahman* maintain with reflection that the entire universe exists by encompassing nothing but the act of breathing (*prāṇana*); for there is no form of Brahman whatsoever other than breathing.
They say, "It is Śabdabrahman. Others maintain that it is the body of Virāj; thus, even the Vairāja is the true reality of Brahman, as it has been said:
Salutation to Him, the Soul of the worlds, whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the sun, and whose ears are the quarters.
And so forth.
"Jāti" (birth) is the general characteristic of great beings (*mahāsattva*), the locus of all virtues.
[Page 61]

The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the *vastu* (the real entity) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Others, however, hold that only the individual objects (*vyakti*), such as physical bodies, are ultimately real; for they argue that there is no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*)—a single entity serving as the substratum for multiple qualities—which either manifests or even logically coheres.
"Verbal usage is fully accomplished by individuals alone; what is the use of a universal (*sāmānya*)?"—

thus disputing over the universal through various conceptual constructions regarding its occurrence, they do not follow after individuals, and asserting many such things as "nothing else that is pervasive appears," they maintain that the genus (*jāti*) is not an ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
They have entered [into this state]; thus, those whose ultimate limit is the aggregate beginning with consciousness are so described.
