This is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*), because in this doctrine of autonomy (*svātantryavāda*), the reality that is manifest cannot be denied; therefore, these distinctions appear as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
But from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these distinctions do not exist at all; they are not distinctions existing by way of intrinsic reality (*satattva*),
such as those imagined by other schools (*tīrthāntara*).

They exist indeed. Therefore, there is only one Supreme Lord of Consciousness (*caitanyamaheśvara*), who is the ultimate reality of supreme light and is autonomous; he shines forth in this or that manner, because there is no manifestation of anything else distinct from him that is not of the nature of light. As it has been said:
Whatever these people, addicted to the practices of heretics, proclaim as the truth based on their own speculative fancies—
that very truth belongs to you; there is nothing else whatsoever.
This dispute among the learned concerns nothing more than mere designations.
Thus [ends the twenty-seventh].
Now, he provides an illustration by means of the capacity of error to convey a non-existent object: "In a rope there is no snake,
yet it causes terror even unto death."
The power of delusion is indeed so great that it cannot be discerned. || 28 ||

The great power, the supreme capacity, of error— which consists in the non-apprehension of fullness— to manifest as something other than its true nature cannot be discerned by anyone; it cannot be discerned by anyone.
It can be investigated— meaning up to this point. For example, when a rope is perceived according to its actual state,
for those who determine "this is a snake" due to the delusion of its length and coiled form,
this determination of a snake is an appearance of a non-existent object even within the substance of the rope, [arising] from the appearance of an existent object.

Fear brings about the end of life; this is established by experience. Who, indeed, has not met with the destruction of their heart through the breaking of the heart while deluded—having mistaken a post for a living being, or having mentally projected a terrifying form? Thus, it is delusion alone that manifests incompleteness.
The cause—thus [it is said]. || 28 ||
This establishes the point at hand:
in the same way, dharma and adharma, birth in heaven or hell, death, happiness, and suffering [are likewise].
And even though caste, stages of life, and so forth do not exist in the Self, they appear due to the power of delusion. || 29 ||

Thus, just as a rope— which is existent in the ultimate sense— is perceived through delusion as a snake and thereby performs the causal function (arthakriyā) associated with a snake, in the very same way, dharma and so forth [arise] in the minds of those who conceive of the body as the self.

Even that which is non-existent (*asad*), being in reality (*tattvataḥ*) non-occurrent, comes into being solely by virtue of delusion (*vibhrama*)—that is, through the power of the bewilderment of *māyā*—and attains existence through the error [thinking], "This alone is the truth. Dharma consists of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and so forth; adharma consists of the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth; heaven (*svaḥ*) is unsurpassed bliss; and hell (*niraya*)...

Torture, birth (arising), death (the absence of birth), pleasure (delight), pain (the agitation born of passion), as well as "I am the color of Brahman" and so forth, and "I am a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī)" and so forth— the inclusion of the word "and so forth" refers to austerity, worship, vows, and all such things whose essence consists merely of mental construction.

It is merely the manifestation of delusion that, through the power of *māyā*, is falsely identified as the self in the form of the body and so forth. All of this originates from error, by which bound souls (*paśu*) partake in an incessant succession of heaven, hell, birth, and death; however, it does not exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
For one's own self, which is a single compact mass of undivided consciousness and bliss, no such thing as merit, demerit, or the like is perceived at all.
Having thus analyzed the capacity of error (*bhrānti*) to manifest unreal objects,
he explains its arising.
This is that darkness which [consists in] the manifestation of entities,
even though they are not distinct from the Self.
This conceit of "self" arises [in relation to what is actually] non-self. || 30 ||

"This is that darkness" refers to this very delusion just described, which consists in the manifestation of fullness as universal bewilderment— that is, [the state] in which all things existing in the universe, appearing in the form of subjects and objects, manifest as such.
"Nothing that is not luminous becomes manifest"—

thus, by the impossibility of manifestation otherwise; for although these entities exist as the very body of luminosity and are non-different from the Great Lord’s consciousness (*caitanya*), there is this [perception] of these objects as being distinct [from the self].

The conceit of non-self (*anātmābhimāna*)—that [objects] are graspable, external, and distinct from me—is the imposition of insentience (*jaḍatva*), which is unreal, upon those objects by casting aside their actual nature as consciousness.
This is the intended meaning: in the manifestation of an entity, there is no manifestation of anything else that is of the nature of non-manifestation.

Since external causes such as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are untenable, self-luminosity itself is autonomous; that is to say, it manifests as blue, pleasure, and so forth. Therefore, [it appears] in the form of both subject and object.
"My very nature as consciousness shines forth"—this which is the real form does not shine;
rather, only unreal duality manifests. Thus, because of the absence of the manifestation of reality, error is described by the metaphor of darkness. || 30 ||

Demonstrating that the conceit of self in what is not-self is preceded by the conceit of non-self in the self, he declares that this delusion is even more of a nature of confusion than mere optical darkness: "This is a darkness even greater than darkness."
This is a great boil upon a tumor:
that one regards as the self even that which is not the self, such as the body, the vital breaths, and so forth. (31)

First of all, even regarding entities whose true nature is that of a single consciousness, the production of duality and insentience has been brought about by the cataract of non-recognition (*akhyāti*); whereby entities that are non-different from one's own self are perceived as distinct from it.
[Page 67]

Expansion; for this very reason, non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is called "darkness" (*timira*), just as even a single moon appears as two moons due to the darkness of a streak in the eye. In the same way, through the darkness of non-apprehension, even the one reality—which is the nature of one's own self—is perceived as manifold and as something other than the self.

It had been illuminated. While it remained thus, another darkness arrived; through delusion, this further delusion has fallen upon me, like the appearance of a carbuncle upon a boil. For, while all objects existing in the universe—whose true nature as consciousness has been cast aside by non-apprehension—have been rendered inert, a separate, extraneous insentient thing has been extracted from among them.

To conceive of oneself as the Self—that is, the identification with what is not the Self—within the fragmented objects of knowledge such as the body, the vital breath, and so forth, thinking "I am thin," "I am fat," "I am hungry," "I am happy," or "I am nothing," while [these] exist as subjects that are not the Self; this is a most grievous error. If, first of all, by means of this conceit of self...

If [consciousness] exists without destruction, let it exist even in the case of blue, pleasure, and so forth; or let it not exist anywhere at all. As for that which [is claimed to exist] in certain insentient things such as the body and the like, which are like clods of earth—[page 68]—[let it be there].

The consecration into the essence of "I-ness" as one's own self, while elsewhere—in objects such as blue or pleasure—the demonstration of non-self through the mode of "this-ness" (idantā): this alone is the full cycle of transmigratory existence that is to be lamented, wherein the blow of dualities, brought about by egoistic conceit, drags down the bound souls (paśus). As it was said by a Yoginī in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
Madālasā saw the vehicle on the ground, and within the vehicle she saw her own body,
and within that body as well, another person was seated.
"One's sense of 'mine-ness' toward the earth is not as great as that which is excessive toward one's own body; this is extreme delusion. (25.18) || 31 ||

Thus, by the power of non-recognition (*akhyāti*), one binds oneself through false conceptualizations; so he says [in the following] regarding the investigation of the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Through the proliferation of the sky of intellectual cognition,
it envelops itself in manifold ways, like a weaver with his net. (32)
[The meaning is that "overpowering" refers to being struck down by duality in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
On page 69:
Every cognizer, whose consciousness has been cast aside by non-apprehension, is bound by the fetters of conceptual constructions arising from itself.
It envelops even the all-pervading Self. How? To this he says: "the body," and so forth.

The investigation of the body and the vital breath; the knowledge and certainty of the intellect (*dhī*); the expansion and proliferation of the spaces (*nabhas*); through their conjunction—that is, through the connection with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the body and so on. For example: "I am thin," "I am stout," and so forth.
"I am handsome and learned"—thus do foolish women, commoners, and farmers, considering themselves somewhat discerning, conceive of the body alone as the self through their own mental construction.
Yet the body perishes right here; how can it possess the nature of a self? Therefore, he who is hungry...
"I am thirsty"—thus think those who identify with the vital breath (prāṇa), while others, considering themselves discerning, [think]:

"The body and the vital breath are insentient like a clod of earth; how could there be the nature of a self (ātman) in these two? Therefore, that which perceives pleasure, pain, and so forth—thinking 'I am happy,' 'I am miserable'—that is the self."
— Thus, even the Mīmāṃsakas and others who identify with the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city) are among those of the highest discernment.
How can this pleasure, pain, and so forth— which are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*)— be spoken of as belonging to the Self?

Therefore, those who hold the conceit of emptiness maintain that the Self is that wherein there is an absence of the conceptual constructs of body, vital breath, and intellect. Likewise, they hold that whatever appears here is not "I"; thus, the Self is merely the void whose nature consists of the negation of everything, being devoid of manifestation, and it is expressed by the word "space" (*nabhas*). That too—

When, at the time of meditative absorption, they experience that which is empty— thinking, "We ourselves are not even this emptiness"— then, establishing another emptiness as their very self, they [say] "not," "not," thereby abandoning each respective emptiness accepted by the proponents of Brahman, and [realizing] that state of being the self of emptiness.

"They grasp [it]"—thus the elaboration regarding the sky (*nabhaḥ-prapañca*) has been explained in the *Kārikā*. In this way, because they do not reach the ultimate limit of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit-svarūpa*), yogins who conceive of the self as empty (*śūnyātma-mānin*) are immersed in the cave of deep sleep; they are merely a continuous stream of insentient matter.
Deluded indeed, they bind even their own nature, which is the very essence of consciousness, with insentience.
How strange—this is a marvel—that such a calamity occurs, for it cannot be brought about by oneself. In this regard:

He provides an illustration with the words "by a net," and so forth. Just as a certain spider or an insect, having constructed a web or a covering out of its own saliva, envelops itself on all sides and binds itself for its own destruction, whereby it later meets its end right there; so too—

One who conceives of the body and so forth as the self, however, binds his very own self through conceptual constructions of "I" and "mine" fashioned by his own imagination. And thus say the Buddhists: "When there is a real self, there is the notion of 'another'."
From the distinction between self and other arise attachment and aversion;
all faults are produced when one is bound by these two.
Thus they say. || 32 ||

"How is this insurmountable great delusion, which arises from the subjectivity of the body and so forth, dissolved?"—the cause for this is none other than the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Lord; thus he says:
[Page 72]
By means of the yoga of illuminating the majesty of one’s own gnosis, one should unravel one’s own self;
thus [is described] the manifold nature of bondage and liberation.
Paramaśiva extends his play. || 33 ||

The "expansion" (*vibhava*) of that knowledge of one's own self— which is characterized by consciousness and consists in the realization of one's own sovereignty— is the intensification of that sovereignty, which takes the form of the wonder of supreme subjectivity (*parāhaṃtā*) within the nature of consciousness through the dissolution of identification with the body and so forth; it is a single, dense mass of consciousness and bliss.

"I am independent"—this is the manifestation (*bhāsana*) of that power (*vibhava*) whose very nature is the sovereignty of consciousness; it is the light (*prakāśa*) [of the realization]: "All this power is mine. It is the appropriation within one's own self of everything that was previously conceived as external. The *yoga* of that [power] is that which occurs within the self through the process of such constant cultivation.

Through the firmness of such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), by means of this union with the manifestation of the glory of one's own knowledge, one unravels one's own self— which is of the nature of consciousness and not derived from anything else— that had previously been enveloped by the shackles of the identification with the body, the vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void.

By the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) that "I am indeed independent, having consciousness as my very nature," the Lord once again effects an uncoiling— that is, He becomes free from all concealment. Thus, [this state] has arisen through the power of non-recognition (*akhyāti*).
"The obscuration of one’s own self by the body and so forth perishes again through the power of [right] cognition;

thus, this much is a defect imagined by one’s own conceptual construction"—this is the certainty established by the venerable author of the *Tantrasāra*: "I am inert, I am bound by karma," as held by the fettered person (*paśu*).
"I am bound, I am impure, I am driven by others"—
by means of the method of attaining a firm resolve that this is otherwise,
the conscious Self, whose body is the universe, immediately becomes the Lord.

Thus [it is asked]: why does the Blessed One bind and release? To this he says: "This is bondage," and so forth. By the sequence previously established, the Blessed One—the independent Supreme Śiva, whose defining characteristic is the single mass of perfect consciousness and bliss—because his nature is to sport in the essence of concealing his own form (*svarūpagopana*), [binds and releases].
Having first brought about the manifestation of non-apprehension, it causes its own self— which has assumed the state of a subject such as the body—
to conceal its true nature and thereby effect bondage; and in that very same way, again, by its own will...

By means of the process of illuminating the knowledge of one's own self, he removes the bondage of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) consisting of the body and so forth, and thus he himself liberates that very self; in this way, in both respects, he extends— that is, he expands— the wondrous play (*krīḍā*) and sport (*khelā*), which consists of the marvelous nature of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and liberation (*apavarga*).

"I do not delight in being alone"—this is indeed the very nature of the Lord, that even when he has entered into various states, being the very form of his own essence, he manifests everywhere as the experiencer; this alone is his sovereignty. || 33 ||
This is not all; rather, the Lord manifests yet another specific state that rests entirely within its own form—thus he says:
"emission, maintenance, and withdrawal."
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep appear within that fourth state (turiya),
yet it shines forth unenveloped by them.

Those specific states such as creation and so forth which exist in relation to the universe, and those particular states such as waking and so forth which reside in the subject of Māyā— both of these [exist] in this Blessed One, who is a mass of bliss, in two ways.
In the fourth abode, the fourth state consisting of the fullness of pure I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), those [entities] shine while resting therein;

they obtain their own essential existence as something external only in relation to the imagined subject. Whatever does not shine upon the wall of the Supreme Lord does not shine even as something external; therefore—
"The fourth [state] should be poured like oil upon the three" (Śivasūtra 3.20).
This is the ultimate truth: that in all states, the form of the Fourth (turya) remains as an underlying thread.
To the question, "By this much, has their own nature been obscured there or not? he says: "Nevertheless..."

"It shines as if not covered by them. Even in this way, although it is covered for the sake of the existence of their own nature (*svarūpasattā*), it nevertheless manifests everywhere as the universal experiencer by virtue of having transcended them;
it does not, however, conceal its full nature there due to that covering—such is the abode of Śiva (*śivadhāma*).
It is always completely full in all states whatsoever. || 34 ||
While describing the nature of the three states— waking and so forth— by means of Vedāntic terminology,
[the text] also reveals the Fourth (turīya), which is superior to them and permeates them.
The waking state is Viśva due to differentiation;
the dream state is Taijasa due to the majesty of illumination;
the deep sleep state is Prājña.
Because it is a mass of pure knowledge, that which follows is the fourth state (turya). || 35 ||
The waking state itself is the universe, the *vairāja* nature of Brahman; why? Because of differentiation:

for all subjects, the activity of the eyes and other senses proceeds toward the fivefold objects such as sound, which are external and created by the Supreme Lord—thus, [this belongs] to the one Brahman alone.
For one who exists in the relationship of object and subject, there is the manifold diversity of sensory cognitions. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"Knowledge is the waking state" (1.8). This is celebrated as the *virāj* state of Brahman, as the Śruti says:
He who has all-seeing eyes and a face on every side, hands on every side, and feet on every side.
The one God, generating heaven and earth, bows with his two arms and with all that is worthy of worship.
Thus, dream is the state of fire (tejas) of Brahman. Why? He says:
"Because of the majesty of light. In a dream, the external organs do not function with regard to objects such as sound, nor does any external sound or the like exist there as an ultimate reality.

Nor is any other cause—whether distinct or non-distinct from ignorance and so forth—perceived as external to the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*), nor is it logically tenable when examined through reasoning; yet, everything manifests in a dream. Therefore, by the force of this fact, it follows that he alone is the Blessed One, one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*).
The Lord, having entered into the respective state of each subject and dreaming,

by the freedom of His own light, divides His very Self into the manifold variety of subjects— such as houses, cities, and watchtowers— and indeed manifests a universe that is unique to each individual subject within the dream. Thus it is said.
The independence of Brahmā [is] precisely in the dream state, as admitted by the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādibhiḥ); for this reason, in the Vedāntas... [page 78] ... [it is so stated].
This has been stated: having divided himself by himself and created various kinds of entities,
the Lord of All, who consists of all things, appears as the enjoyer in a dream.
Thus, the very greatness of manifestation is the reason here; therefore, the dream state is the *tejo-avasthā* (luminous state) of Brahman.

Likewise, the *prājña* is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). That which is the state of deep sleep for all subjects is the *prajña*; thus, the *prājña-avasthā* is the state of Brahman. For this reason:

Because the proliferation of the grasped and the grasper has dissolved for all subjects, when there is the dissolution of the grasped and so forth into the nature of the Great Void— which is a state of deep sleep where only latent impressions remain— the wisdom of Brahman itself, which is the seed of the universe, remains as the innermost knower; this is what is meant by "of everything."

This is the ground of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) for the cognizer’s manifestation of the manifold diversity of the universe, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth; for we observe that once awakened from this state, he engages in worldly activity just as he did previously. Otherwise, if Brahman—which is by nature the stable cognizer and which encompasses everything—had not shone forth upon this ground, how [could this be]?
Then,
for the cognizer who has arisen [from that state]— [regarding] the object previously experienced— it is "just so" by way of having been experienced as such.
Memory would have arisen; nor would there have appeared the experience: "I slept happily," "I slept painfully," or "I was deeply unconscious. And thus says Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa:
If all objects experienced within were not well-guarded by being assimilated into your own self,
they would take on the nature of a non-deceptive realization of reality.
then no such thing as memory could possibly exist.
Thus, it is proclaimed that deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is the state of the *prājña* [the "knower"] of Brahman, consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*). Why?
Because it is a mass of knowledge (*jñānaghana*). This reason applies equally to both deep sleep and the fourth state (*turya*), as it should be understood in both cases.
This plane of deep sleep is a mass of knowledge, whose form is light, and is purely...
Being obscured by the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the universal dissolution (*viśvapralaya*), it does not become pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmayī*).
As it is said in the *Spandaśāstra*:
"Endowed with the supreme power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge..."
The All-pervasive Lord shines in two ways; elsewhere, however, He consists of pure consciousness.
(Nirvāṇa Tantra 1.18) [The word *dhyāmala* means unclear or indistinct.]

Thus it is said: "Beyond that is the Fourth (turya). Therefore, beyond that state of deep sleep (suṣupta), there is another, which—due to the complete destruction of the latent impressions and tendencies of all animal-like bonds—is the Fourth form of Brahman, consisting of pure and perfect bliss; this is its appropriate name. As for the name used here, it is not merely literal in its etymological sense.

It arises; therefore, it is the ground of rest for the three explained states, pervading them as the innermost of all. Thus, by completing the number four, the designation "the Fourth" (*turya*) is applied here by means of the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*). How [is this so] regarding the three states?
"Is this [state] also continuous beyond that?"—to this he says: "Because of its density of consciousness (*jñānaghanatvāt*).

Since all states such as waking and so forth consist of ignorance for subjects because they are inclined toward duality, whereas the fourth state (*turya*) results from the complete exhaustion of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the agitation between the grasped and the grasper.

It is the embodiment of the bliss of the light of the mass of consciousness (*jñānaghana*); therefore, although it resides within those states, it is "other" and supreme because it transcends them by virtue of being composed of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*). Thus, it is Brahman alone—the independent, supreme non-dual nature—which, variegated by these states, unfolds as the full plenitude. || 35 ||

Even so, since the pure Supreme Self exists as the thread running through all subjects, it necessarily undergoes the impurity of non-recognition (*akhyāti*) inherent in the multitude of subjects; this is what [the opponent] suggests.
That is not so; this he makes known by means of an illustration: "Just as the expanse of the sky is not truly defiled by clouds, smoke, or dust."
In the same way, the Supreme Person remains untouched by the transformations of māyā. || 36 ||

Just as the surface of the sky, though clouds, smoke, and masses of dust may occupy it, is not rendered impure by them— since it is pure by its very nature— nor is its eternal vastness ever diminished; rather, like reflections in a mirror, the sky remains simply the sky, appearing variegated according to those various conditions.

Because He is always recognized as being suchness (*tathātva*). "In that same way" means that the Lord is not touched by the transformations of Māyā arising from non-recognition (*akhyāti*), which consist of various diverse states such as birth and death residing in manifold subjects—even though these [transformations] reside in the Lord. The Lord is not affected by them.

His essential nature is not taken away by them; for he alone is the Supreme Person (*para-puruṣa*), the primordial manifestation and the place of rest for all persons—that is, all individual souls (*jīva*)—and thus, by virtue of being the experiencer of all, [he remains as such].
*page 82*

"It always vibrates"—thus it is designated by the word *para* (the Supreme). Therefore, there is no impairment whatsoever of the Blessed One by the transformations of *māyā*, which are non-luminous in nature and arise from Himself, like a magician’s illusions;
for this reason, it was stated by the Supreme Lord (*Parameṣṭhin*) even in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*:

Although the stability of objects is restricted to the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), even there it is ultimately established in the Supreme Self.
"How could there be any restraint upon that [Self] by means of the vital breath, since it exists by its very own nature?
Thus [ends verse 36].

But surely, if persons are ultimately nothing but pure consciousness, how is it that they partake in the manifold variety of specific states such as pleasure, pain, delusion, birth, and death? To this, he provides an illustration:
Just as when the space within one jar is pervaded by dust, the others do not become soiled, so it is with these.
Living beings experience the distinctions of pleasure and pain. || 37 ||

Just as when the space within one jar is covered by a mass of dust, the other spaces within jars do not become soiled by that dust— even though they are naturally pure— because there is no difference in their nature as space.

They exist as follows: for just as the sky—which is pure, all-pervading, and eternal—becomes contracted by the confinement of a jar, it remains exactly like that only for that specific jar; it does not follow, however, that all the spaces within jars, cloths, and so forth become perfumed with black agallochum incense.

Just as scents such as musk or the fragrance of jasmine do not become mixed because they possess the singular nature of space, due to being delimited by the jars and other objects contained within them;

on the contrary, while the one real space remains present even in a single location, jars and other things—being constrained by the contraction of their own respective walls—manifest a diversity of spaces. Thus...

Just as the very contraction produced by a jar remains as the sky because it performs causal function (*arthakriyā*) as such [the sky], so too this impurity or the like residing in the jar does not serve to conceal the essential nature of the sky,
nor do those things delimited by jars and the like conceal one another.
"The mingling of skies"— in the same way, these individual souls (*jīva*),

though their ultimate reality is nothing but the one pure consciousness (*ekacinmātra-pāramārtha*), [are affected] by the *āṇava* [impurity] through the supreme Lord’s power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).
— By being enveloped by the three sheaths consisting of *māyā* and *prakṛti*, their essential nature— which is full, pervasive, and a single mass of consciousness-bliss—
is cast aside and rendered limited; whereby, although they are essentially one consciousness,
they become mutually distinct due to the wretchedness of the fragmentation caused by the three sheaths inherent within themselves.

Like the space within a jar or a cloth; thus, it is only the fragmentation produced by the sheath of *māyā* that is conventionally designated as the "individual soul" (*jīva*). However, in the Supreme Lord—who is a single, undivided mass of consciousness and bliss—there is no such conventional usage as seen in other philosophical systems, such as "souls," "persons," "selves," or "atoms. Thus...

The individual souls (jīvas), delimited by the sheaths beginning with the atomic (āṇava), possess various bodies perfumed by the impressions of diverse karmic impurities from time immemorial; they possess various dispositions and partake in the manifold distinctions of the dualities of merit and demerit, heaven and hell, pleasure and pain, birth and death, and so forth.

The pure [entities] do not become intermingled with one another, just as the spaces delimited by jars and other objects are perfumed by various substances; thus it is well-established that even though they have consciousness alone as their ultimate reality, they possess mutual difference due to their own delimitations. || 37 ||

Thus, those particular states residing within the sphere of the individual soul (jīva-maṇḍala) are merely attributed metaphorically to the Blessed Lord; they do not exist here in reality at all— so he says.
When [the Lord] is tranquil, he appears as if tranquil;
when delighted, he is delighted; and when possessed by delusion, he is deluded—such is the Blessed One while the multitude of principles exists.
But in the ultimate sense, it is not so.

When the group of principles—the collection of senses—is tranquil and ceased, the Supreme Self residing therein is perceived as if tranquilized or lost; likewise, when that [group] is joyful and full of delight, He is similarly characterized;
but when it is filled with supreme darkness and deluded, He is considered deluded—as in the case of the stationary species, and not otherwise.

In the ultimate sense, according to the actual state of things, that Supreme Lord exists in that manner. For every insentient portion is subject to being produced or withdrawn; however, in the eternal Blessed One, whose nature is consciousness and who is merely invested with the coverings such as *māyā*, there can be no destruction or origination—thus, O Blessed One, he is always so.
He is equanimous. || 38 ||
The delusion that arose through the process of manifestation is further utterly uprooted by the process of realization; in this regard, he says that this is the very sovereignty of one's own self—
page 86.
Having previously refuted that appearance of the form of that [object] even in what is not the self,
[one now refutes] the form of the non-self in the self.
The Supreme Self shatters delusion. || 39 ||

Having first rejected that appearance of form— which consists of the apprehension of the non-self as the self, such as "I am thin" or "I am fat"— with respect to the body and so forth, which are characterized by insentience and are not the self, [one realizes]: "I am of the nature of the undivided mass of consciousness-bliss, whose essence is unlimited."

And being "independent" (*svatantra*), by means of the flashing forth of unartificial *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), one seizes away the artificial subjectivity of the body and so forth; thus, the Self itself, having shed the bond of the body and attained the state of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatā*), [perceives] that delusion which occurs regarding this very Self— the manifesting form, the essence of light, wherein all worldly objects appear like its own limbs.

The manifestation of duality produced by the conceit of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) with respect to the body and so forth— that [conceit] he shatters, [realizing]: "I alone am one, as the self of the universe."

"I am vibrating"—thinking thus, he pulverizes [the world]. This is the intended meaning here: as long as the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the non-self, such as the body and so forth, has not dissolved, so long will the delusion of the manifestation of duality (*bhedaprathāmoha*) not vanish, even within the universe which is essentially the manifestation of one's own Self. Therefore, through the destruction of the error of the conceit of self regarding the non-self, [the delusion ceases].

Only the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord who is the Great Lord of one's own self, destroys the delusion of the conceit of "self" regarding what is not-self; no other has the power to do so in this matter. || 39 ||
Thus, for the yogin who has become the Supreme Goddess through the removal of these two types of delusion, no further task remains— so he says: "In this way, the pair of delusions..."
For the supreme yogin who has accomplished his purpose through the total eradication of the root [of afflictions], there never arises any further calculation of duties to be performed. || 40 ||

In this manner, by the method set forth in the meaning of the *kārikā*, for one who has accomplished their purpose through the tearing asunder of the sprout of the two-fold delusion, of their own sovereignty—
[page 88] —

For one who has accomplished the attainment of the goal— the acquisition of the supreme human purpose— through the complete shattering of all contraction by means of thorough realization, and who is thus engaged in preeminent yoga, there is never any further duty such as wandering to sacred fords,
occupying holy sites, initiation, recitation, meditation, or exposition.
Even the mental activity that conceives of remaining duties in the form of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth does not exist;

for this alone is the supreme dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga. Thus, the primacy belongs to the yoga of one's own Self; therefore, once that is attained, there is no further exertion required elsewhere.
[This concerns] the perfected yogi. As it has been said:
"When your intellect shall transcend the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard" (2.52).
Thus it is said in the Gītās. 40.
Now, through the immersion into the Śākta plane— which consists of both difference and non-difference— of the universe that manifests as differentiated, beginning from earth and ending with Māyā...
[page 89] ...[continues].

Having described the attainment of identity with that [state] through the dissolution of duality by means of reaching the Śāmbhava state— which is a mass of full light and bliss— [the text continues]: "Then,
from that Śāmbhava state, which is like a completely full ocean of nectar..."

Manifesting as the various forms of the breaking waves of the expansion of Śakti, which resembles a great current— beginning with the outpouring of the flow of Śakti— it is the essence of the potency of the Great Mantra (mahāmantra) established through one's own experience, the supreme emergence of non-duality that dissolves all duality, consisting of Nara, Śakti, and...

Intending to gradually unfold the heart of supreme consciousness, which consists of the state of identity with Śiva, he first declares their unification through the reasoning that synthesizes the universe as consisting of the three sections of the Āgama:
"Earth, Prakṛti, and Māyā."
This triad, having fallen into the state of being an object of cognition,
indeed remains as pure existence alone through the power of the contemplation of non-duality. (41)

That which consists of the cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) of the earthly, the elemental, and the illusory (māyīya), having a threefold nature— gross, subtle, and supreme— has fallen into the state of being an object of knowledge and has become the domain of cognition.
Knowledge manifests externally and internally in the form of this or that object;
apart from knowledge, there is no existence of objects, and therefore the world is of the nature of knowledge.
For no entities have ever been made objects by anyone apart from cognition;
therefore, it is concluded that cognition has attained the nature of those very entities.

Thus, by the principle stated in the *Śrīkālikākrama*, through the power—that is, the excellence—of that non-dual contemplation (*advaitabhāvanā*), [reality] becomes nothing but pure existence (*sanmātra*), which is the remainder after all else has vanished, consisting solely of the nature of manifestness (*prakāśamānatā*) and the nature of pure being (*sattāmātra*). The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). || 41 ||
He establishes this very point with the intention of demonstrating the unreality of difference:
"Just as gold is seen when the distinctions of the girdle, the earring, and the bracelet are abandoned."
In the same way, when difference is abandoned, everything appears as pure Being alone. || 42 ||

Just as, for instance, a golden ornament such as a girdle appears merely as gold to one seeking gold, setting aside its specific form as a girdle; and just as it appears as mere metal to one seeking only that much, whether it be gold, silver, bronze, copper, lead, or the like— in the same way, all this [is perceived].
Of the yogin who has abandoned the stains of conceptual constructions such as "abandoning" and "taking up," and who abides solely in non-conceptual appearance.
"Through transformation within form and the other [objects], its establishment occurs.
According to this principle stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa, when duality is abandoned, that which is pure being, whose essence is mere existence, shines forth. 42.

Therefore, by abandoning the appearance of contraction regarding all this, and by means of what is well-known from the scriptures, he speaks— casting a glance toward the tradition of mantra which involves the ascent of the human form into the Śākta form—
that Brahman is supreme and pure.
Peaceful, non-dual in nature, equal, and all-encompassing—
the immortal truth rests within the radiant Śakti.
All this, whose nature is pure existence, is Brahman because of its vastness; as those who know the Upanishads have said: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."
Thus, it is supreme because of its fullness; it is pure because of the absence of anything to be rejected or accepted;
it is tranquil because of the subsiding of all separateness; and for that very reason, it consists of non-duality.
It is equal because it is devoid of excellence or deficiency; even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its universal form, and it is beyond conceptualization.
Thus, by virtue of this state, everything is immortal—that is, indestructible.
However, regarding the two portions—the real and the unreal—which are established in every individual entity:
that which is real therein is the genus (*jāti*), while the unreal are the individuals (*vyakti*) that exist.
Thus:

"That which is at the beginning, that which is at the end, and that which is in the middle—that is its reality. According to this principle established by the venerable Bhartṛhari, it is the Truth; and that alone is this [reality] whose nature consists of pure existence (*sattāmātra*).

Everything rests within the supreme power, which is of the nature of the equilibrium of the powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action, and whose form is luminosity; for the determination of objects is grounded in consciousness.
Thus, by remaining [in this state], one becomes identical with that.
Furthermore, there is the "peaceful" (śānta), which is the cerebral form at the end of the letter *śa*; beyond that is the "immortal" (*amṛta*), which consists of the seed-syllable of immortality.

Brahman consists solely of pure existence (*sanmātra*); it is pure through contact with the state known as *sādākhya*. For this very reason, because it brings all things into a state of equal flavor (*samarasīkaraṇa*)—thinking "I am all this"—it is both equal (*sama*) and all-encompassing (*sakala*). And for this reason, it is called *akhyāti*.

Because it flows forth, it is true; that which was taught by the Blessed One as the third Brahman, O fair-hipped one—thus it is stated in the *Śrītriṃśikā*. This very [state] is touched by the nature of immortality and has ascended to the station of Sadāśiva.
This Brahman, which consists of the universe, comes to rest within the power previously mentioned. || 43 ||
That which does not rest within the supreme power by way of action, knowledge, and will is nothing at all;
thus he says:
"it is desired" and "it is known."
And it is brought about in the form of light;
yet even that sky which is untouched [by conceptualization] attains the state of being a flower. (44)

Whatever object exists externally according to the nature of things, if it is [perceived] by means of a radiant consciousness— consisting of the expansion of the Supreme Power (parā-śakti) which is the equilibrium of these three powers through the channels of will, knowledge, and action— then...

That which is not grasped, devoid of both manifestation and description, is like a flower in the sky. By this, the potency (*vīrya*) of the state consisting of the trident situated above the sphere of existence (*sadvṛtti*) is indicated. || 44 ||

Describing his immersion into this state of Śakti, he manifests the process of becoming one with it through the attainment of the state of Śambhu, by means of the circumambulation of the trident of Śakti.
Through yoga, even the entire [universe] is dissolved by the God of gods into the Supreme Lord, the ultimate reality named Śiva. 45.

Thus, all of this, because its nature is pure existence (*sattāmātra*), is the ultimate reality of the aforementioned Brahman; through the application of the method established by the logic of the penetration of the trident of powers (*śakti-triśūla-parigama*),
by means of the sequence of absorption into the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), within the ultimate reality named Śiva.

In the Supreme Lord, who is the single mass of undivided consciousness, within His own essential nature, [the world] is emitted—through the intensity of inward-turned reflective awareness and by means of absorption in that [nature].
[8] *Prakhyā* is knowledge; *upākhyā* is verbal expression; or else, [it is] from one's own self...
*Prakhyā* is the desire to attain the state of becoming an object of knowledge; *upākhyā* is the desire to cause another to attain the state of becoming an object of knowledge;
the meaning is the wish to enter into the state of being an object for the manifestation of both oneself and others.
One is brought to a state of identification with that [reality]— namely, with the gods beginning from Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva,
as well as with all the luminous senses— by the Lord, Paramaśiva himself; for it is not otherwise here.
The agency of any other whatsoever is untenable, nor is there any other cognizer distinct from this [Lord];

rather, it is precisely this Blessed One, ascending through various stages, who manifests in the form of various cognizers such as Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas). Thus, the statement "by the God of gods" is entirely appropriate.
Thus, the function of emission (visarga) has been demonstrated. || 45 ||

Thus, having demonstrated by way of conclusion that the world— which is of the nature of difference and consists of individual beings— attains a state of identity with Śiva, who is a single mass of non-dual consciousness, through its superimposition upon the Śākta plane which is characterized by both difference and non-difference, [the author now proceeds].

Śiva alone, as a single mass of consciousness, having manifested in the form of Śakti, flashes forth as the universal form consisting of the individual soul (nara); yet there is no form of Śakti or nara whatsoever apart from Śiva, for it is Śiva himself who thus flashes forth through the coagulation of his own essence— this is the logic of expansion, consisting of the unfolding of the Great Mantra.
It demonstrates—
page 96—
furthermore, the five powers.
Through the process of expansion,
that [power] also externally creates the three variegated eggs by attaining its own nature outside. || 46 ||

That which is Paramaśiva, whose nature is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the five powers known as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), by means of the method of unfolding the levels (*bhūmikā*) called Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā— which consist in the manifestation of the predominance of those powers such as consciousness— [produced] that triad of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍatraya*).
"Variegated" (*vicitra*) means that which has been created in the form of various worlds and so forth, having attained external existence;
that is, by the manifestation of one's own self through the nature of external appearance. By the word "again," he shows this:
that Supreme Śiva alone, being autonomous, always [manifests] upon his own foundation.

Displaying the play of manifesting and dissolving the entire cosmic expansion—as if it were something distinct from Himself, though it is not distinct from His own Self—He remains in this manner; for there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from Him. || 46 ||
Thus, the Blessed One, whose nature is the play of manifesting and dissolving the universe—
[he who is] designated as Śiva— who is he, where does he abide, or by what [means]?

Anticipating the objection, "Is this established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?", he demonstrates through words denoting the word "we" (*asmad-śabda*) that Śiva, who is one's very own self, manifests everywhere as primordially established and brings about creation and the other cosmic processes.
Thus, the Lord, driving the machine of the wheel of powers through the yoga of play, [realizes]:
"I alone am the pure form."
He stands in the position of the lord of the great wheel of powers (śakti-mahācakra). || 47 ||
The entire universe shines within me alone, like jars and other objects in a stainless mirror; everything emanates from me.
Like the variety of dreams [appearing] from one who is asleep. || 48 ||
I alone am the universal form,
like a body whose nature consists of hands, feet, and so forth;
I alone am in everything.
I manifest within all things like a radiant form. || 49 ||
The seer, the hearer, and the smeller, though devoid of body and senses, is nonetheless a non-doer.
I alone compose the various established doctrines, scriptures, and logical arguments.

In this manner— as explained— He impels that very machine, which is the infinite multitude of powers projected by the fivefold powers beginning with *cit*, through the application of play (*krīḍā-yoga*),
according to the logic of a waterwheel (*araghaṭṭa-ghaṭīyantra*), by means of the effortless sequence of emerging and submerging in creation and the other cosmic processes.

Turning it over [within himself], [he realizes]: "I alone am the God of all living beings; I am the unstruck sound (*anāhata-nāda*), whose essence is the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā-camatkāra-sāra*), the self-reflection of one's own nature. It is this very self of everyone, which cannot be denied, that shines forth as the playful God. By this—

It has been established that Śiva is established solely in his own essential nature (*svasvarūpaniṣṭha*). Likewise, he is of pure form (*śuddharūpa*), whose sphere of experience transcends all conceptual construction (*kalpanātikrāntagocara*). Furthermore, there is the state of the Lord of the Great Wheel (*mahācakranāyakapada*), which bestows upon the powers—the deities of the senses—the sovereignty over the activities of grasping and abandoning objects.

He who abides therein is "tatstha" (established in that). Since the functional powers of the senses possess no ontological existence apart from their repose in consciousness, one must seek the possessor of those powers (*śaktimant*) alone in order to attain one's true nature.
By the phrase "they worship incessantly," the Lord's status as the presiding deity of specific worlds is set aside, because He is the presiding deity of the hearts of all subjects. Likewise,
whatever is conceived as the universe, all that shines within me alone, according to the analogy of reflections in a mirror.
In other words, it shines forth as resting precisely within the meaning of "I" (asmad-artha) whose nature has been explained, and it pulsates with the very essence of "I-ness" (ahantā).

Likewise, from "me"—that is, from the full Self whose form is "I"—this entire universe without exception flows forth; that is to say, it manifests as being withdrawn [into itself] in relation to the subject.

How so? He says: "Like the variety of dreams from one who is asleep. Just as for a cognizer who is fast asleep, in the state of dreaming, there appears a manifold wonder consisting of cities, walls, temples, and so forth—the variety of dream-objects—even though external objects are absent.

Because there is no other cause imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, it proceeds having self-consciousness (*svasaṃvit*) alone as its material cause; likewise, because no other cause prescribed by other philosophical systems (*tīrthāntara*) is tenable, the universe arises from the form "I" (*aham*), which is a single, undivided mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*). Thus, it is "I" alone.
"Viśvarūpaḥ," and so forth.
That full awareness of consciousness which is "I"— this alone am I.

Having attained the state of subjectivity in various bodies and so forth, he is "universal in form" (*viśvarūpa*); that is to say, because he manifests through internal differentiation even among cowherds, children, women, and others, all things are indeed my own forms. Like what? Like a body whose nature consists of hands, feet, and so on; just as, in a general sense, there is one single body for all.
The nature of hands, feet, and so forth is manifold in form according to each individual cognizer due to their specific characteristics;
likewise, the single reality characterized by consciousness is universal in form because it is the abode of all.
Thus, within this entire world consisting of cognizers, means of knowledge, and objects of knowledge, it is I alone who shine forth as everything.
Because it manifests as the experiencer of its own self. How so? "As the luminous form among objects.

Just as among various things a luminous form—a substance characterized by an excellence of radiance—shines intensely, even so, in this inert world, there is the thought: "I am the one whose nature is consciousness. And for this reason, [it is called] "the Seer," and so forth.

Although devoid of body and senses, because I am the very embodiment of consciousness, it is I alone who sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches; thus, through resting in the fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) everywhere, there is the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*). For it is only the aggregate of body and senses that [is said to] "see."

Thus he thinks, and so forth, because in states such as deep sleep there is an absence of being a seer and so on; therefore, [the Self] is the manifestor of the aggregate consisting of the body, senses, and other factors, yet even when devoid of them, it is a single mass of consciousness and bliss.
The Person alone moves within the hearts of all beings. And thus says the Śruti:
"Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper;
he sees without eyes, and he hears without ears."
"He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him;
him they call the foremost, the Great Puruṣa" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19).
Likewise, [it is said] that the Siddhānta Āgama is "even though not an agent," and so forth, [and that] the Lord and the Sage, even though not themselves creators...

"Pervaded by the intention of [beings] such as humans, with the desire to speak both in brief and in detail, and possessing an internal nature of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), I perform various wonders such as the established doctrines (*siddhānta*); however, it is not possible for inert things like the body and senses— which are comparable to clods of earth— to perform such actions."
"Through each respective mediation, I alone am the creator of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By this, it would be stated that neither the utility nor the application of a means of valid cognition is possible regarding the existence of the Great Lord who is one's own self, whose nature is the supreme *Ahaṃtā*. Thus, "I" is indeed such that it cannot be denied.
As the experiencer—
[page 102]—
Śiva alone, as one's own self, is present everywhere in all means of valid cognition.
"Established from the beginning. || 47 || 48 || 49 || 50 ||

Thus, by means of the sequence explained in this way, the yogi becomes the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, firmly reflecting upon his own self with the realization, "All this manifestation is mine. Thus he says:
"In this manner, regarding dualistic conceptualization..."
Having transcended the deluding illusion,
one may sportfully attain absorption in Brahman, just as water merges into water or milk into milk.

In this manner, through the reasoning of constant cultivation of the state of universal "I-ness," when dualistic conceptualization has been swallowed— that is, when the manifestation of duality has dissolved— one transcends delusive *māyā*, which consists of the non-recognition (*akhyāti*) that takes the form of the conceit of self in what is not-self and is the cause for the manifestation of duality, [realizing]: "I alone am the Self of the universe."

Having completely cast off contraction through its dissolution, the man of knowledge (jñānī) should become absorbed in his own nature— which is Brahman, expansive by essence, full, and a single mass of consciousness-bliss— through the dissolution of contraction, thereby attaining identity with Brahman.

One should go. In what manner? To this he says: "In water," and so forth. Just as water—or milk—drawn up from water by various jars and other vessels, though mixed with thousands of different cows such as the *Śāvaleya* and *Bāhuleya*, [remains distinct] once again...

Through the complete dissolution of the contraction of distinctions created by [limiting adjuncts] such as a jar or a brindled cow, just as water enters into water or milk into milk— that single reality alone remains, and no distinction manifests therein; in the same way, through the destruction of the reflective awareness consisting of the body, vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void, one becomes Brahman itself.
As Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa has said: "When the island of the perception of the body has collapsed upon birth,
one attains oneness in the stainless ocean of consciousness."
But you, the inner Self of all, being eternal and one, shine forth when the collection of senses has not been turned back.
Thus ends the Kakṣyā-stotra, [verse] 51.

Thus, for the yogin who has ascended to the state of Brahman, even the overcoming of dualities is composed of Brahman itself and does not prevail to cause the destruction of his true nature; so he says: page 104 ... When the collection of principles has thus attained the state of being identical with Śiva through meditative cultivation,
what grief is there, and what delusion?
For one who perceives everything as Brahman. || 52 ||

In this manner, when the yogin— whose binding of the sheaths has dissolved— attains the state of being identical with Śiva through the firm realization that "all this is one's own single consciousness" by means of contemplation upon the collection of principles (tattva), which is the aggregate of the elements, objects, and senses; and having thus reached the state of supreme non-duality, [the following occurs].

For one who perceives all this multitude of principles as Brahman, there are none at all of those things characterized by grief and delusion or overcome by dualities; because everything is composed of Brahman, they are all of the nature of one’s own true self, and thus they do not lead to distress. || 52 ||

Now, one might ask: "Even for a knower whose nature is supreme non-duality, why should there not necessarily be an accumulation of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious karma caused by that [body], as long as the body remains?"—to this, he provides the following response:
page 105 [The text continues with the response.]
The fruit of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
arises solely from association with false knowledge; for the defect of association is indeed treacherous.
The application of the thief is like that of one who is not a thief. || 53 ||

Even the accumulation of the results of meritorious and non-meritorious actions, such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or the killing of a Brahmin, arises solely from association with false knowledge—namely, that which is preceded by the conceit of self in what is not-self, thinking: "I am the embodied one; let this horse sacrifice and so forth be my means."

In the self, there is a perverted cognition characterized by the conceit of "non-self"; the attachment resulting from that very [cognition] leads to the accumulation of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious karma for the bound soul (paśu), by which it becomes a vessel for the afflictions of saṃsāra, being incessantly permeated by them. Now, one might ask: even though the cognizer is essentially Brahman, why is this so?
Does one thus attain the state of a beast?— to this he introduces another point with the words "For [it is] uneven," and so forth.
Because the fault of attachment is entirely unbearable, just as association with the wicked is for even the most virtuous person.
Just as one attributes one's own faults [to another], so too for the pure cognizer,
the association with delusion born of non-apprehension (akhyāti) brings about the state of a bound soul (paśutva) and bestows the connection with auspicious and inauspicious karma. || 53 ||

Even birth, death, and so forth do not belong to the yogin whose nature is Brahman, but rather only to those subjects who are under the influence of *māyā*; thus he says [of those] who perform worldly transactions.
Those fools who here worship ignorance go from birth to death,
bound by the bolts of merit and demerit. (54)
Those knowers who, identifying the body as the self and being defiled by the desire for fruits,
resort in this world to Māyā— which consists of worldly conduct, is composed of merit and demerit, and takes the form of the manifestation of duality—
as a means for attaining results such as heaven and hell, are deluded and ignorant.

Bound by the shackles of merit and demerit, they are born and die again and again for the sake of experiencing their fruits; thus they remain subjects of the incessant afflictions of saṃsāra. However, the yogi—whose veil of delusion is utterly destroyed, whose bonds of dharma and adharma have dissolved, and whose nature is Brahman—is not born again.
Or one dies—thus [it is said]. || 54 ||
Thus, even those karmas acquired through ignorance are destroyed solely by the manifestation of knowledge and not otherwise; so he says: "accumulated during the time of ignorance."
Even karma, consisting of both dharma and adharma,
perishes through the power of the light of wisdom, like cotton that has been accumulated for a long time. || 55 ||

That action, consisting of merit and demerit, which was accumulated and accepted during the time of ignorance— the occasion of the conceit of being a limited, artificial subject— out of a desire for corresponding fruits, perishes by the power of the light of realization, that is, by the power of the light of specific knowledge [in the form]: "I alone am the Supreme Brahman."

Cognition is capable of burning away the state of being a constructed subject; through the power of its repeated reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), that [state] goes to non-appearance. Like what? He says:
like cotton accumulated over a long time, such as the down of a swan (*haṃsaroma*) accumulated over a long time.

Just as [fuel] is instantly reduced to ashes by the power of a blazing fire, in the same way, the entire accumulation of the fruits of karma is [reduced to ashes] by the power of the fire of primordial wisdom (*vijñāna*).
"In an instant, it goes to destruction. As it is said in the Gītā: "Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes" (4.37).
Thus [ends the verse]. 55.
Not only does previously performed karma dissolve through the clarity of knowledge,
but even present karma, by means of a vision kindled by knowledge, does not culminate in the experience of its fruit— thus he says:
Since even that which has been performed does not lead to fruit once knowledge is attained, how could there be rebirth for one whose connection to the bonds of birth has ceased?
The sun of Śiva shines with his own rays. || 56 ||

When the reflective awareness of one's own nature as the Great Lord has taken root, even actions such as good or evil performed previously are not capable of yielding corresponding fruits, because of the absence of the conceit of being a limited, artificial subject; thus,
due to the absence of the fruit of action, there is no birth suitable for its experience.
In what manner could existence possibly remain for him; rather, the meaning is that there is no rebirth for the yogin.
Now, if he is not born again after the falling away of the body (*piṇḍapāta*), then what would he be like? To this, the author says: "one whose birth has passed," and so forth.
He whose connection—that is, the bond consisting of birth and form—has departed is thus described;

with the veil of delusion destroyed, that Sun in the form of Śiva shines and vibrates by means of his own rays, which are a mass of the light of consciousness. Furthermore, his liberation is not something to be attained elsewhere, as imagined by other schools of thought. Thus it is said.
It is simply that, through the destruction of the contraction produced by the sheaths (kañcuka) such as Māyā and the rest, it attains the state of the full expansion of its own powers.
— Thus [ends verse 56].
Regarding this very point, he states the reasoning:
"Just as a seed, when freed from its husk, shell, and awn, produces a sprout."
Indeed, the self, being liberated from the atomic, the illusory, and the karmic [impurities], is not at all like the sprout of worldly existence. 57.
[The sense is that the Mīmāṃsakas consider the mere attainment of worlds such as heaven to be liberation.
Just as a grain of rice, when separated from its awn, husk, and chaff...

Just as a seed, due to the absence of the totality of conditions such as its own nature and the husk, does not become the cause for the effect characterized by the production of a sprout even when situated amidst earth, water, and sunlight; likewise, [the soul] remains so because of the *āṇava* impurity acting as the husk, the *māyīya* impurity acting as the chaff, and the *kārmika* impurity acting as the outer husk.

The liberated and distinct Self, being devoid of the causal complex consisting of the three impurities, does not again produce the sprout of existence— the growth of saṃsāra; it merely [perceives] within itself the manifold variety of the appearance and disappearance of the multitude of diverse objects throughout the universe.
By contemplating [this], one becomes Maheśvara himself. || 57 ||
Thus, for the man of knowledge whose seed-sheath has been burnt by the fire of wisdom, there is no occasion for doubt regarding anything to be rejected or accepted; therefore, it is said:
"The knower of the Self [has nothing to fear] from any quarter."
For everything indeed appears as his own form;
he does not grieve at all because,
in the ultimate sense, there is no destruction.

He who knows the Self—that is, he who knows the sovereign freedom of his own Great Lord (Maheśvara) as his very self—fears nothing whatsoever; he does not take fright from any king, enemy, or living beings. Why is this so? To this, he says:

"For everything is his own form," because for him— who knows the non-duality of his own Self as the Great Lord— all this collection of objects, this universe, is the form, that is, the appearance, of his own Self alone, whose sole body is the Great Light; since light pervades everything, it is Light itself [that appears] through its sovereignty.
It manifests as both self and other; therefore, whatever appears in the world as a source of fear is, for it, just like its own limb.

How could that which is essentially its own limb produce fear? For only an object distinct from one's own self could be a cause of fear. But what, indeed, could be distinct from that which is entirely complete and devoid of any limiting boundary?

Yama and the others exist, because even a man of knowledge (*jñānin*), though he has cast aside the conceit of identifying the body with the self, might still be afraid; thus, everywhere— [as stated on] page 112—
because of the realization of one's own true nature, even while situated in *saṃsāra*, [the yogi remains] alone, through the dissolution of the distinction between self and other.
He indeed moves about without hesitation, as stated by the venerable Parameṣṭhin:
"O Lord, he who perceives this entire circle of objects, which is free from conceptual construction, as Your very body..."
When the world is filled by his own self alone,
how can there be fear for him who is eternally blissful?
(From the *Utpalastotrāvalī*, Stotra 13, Verse 16:
"The author [of the verse] also says: 'In this cycle of existence, I am alone... [The rest of the verse follows].)
I am distressed by the essence of fear and violence;
yet, established in the thought, "I am alone— what other is there for me?", I remain thus free from fear.

Thus it is said: "And furthermore, he does not grieve," and so forth. Nor does the knower of the Self grieve as others do—thinking, "My wealth, wife, and so forth have perished; I am destitute; I am overcome by disease; I am dying," and so on—because, according to the sequence already explained, in the ultimate, real reality which is of the nature of consciousness, [he perceives nothing else].
When [the mind] is turned inward toward the pure subject alone—
[as on page 113]—
destruction, which is the nature of decay, does not exist; for everything has pride as its essence.

That which appears as an effect, delimited by "thisness" (idantā), arises and perishes; however, this is not the case for the Self, which consists of consciousness, whose essence is the "I-sense" (ahantā), which is uncreated and autonomous—since no effort directed toward action is perceived therein. Nor does its essential nature suffer any loss of integrity on account of this.

For the yogin who reflects in this way, even while remaining within the body, the manifestation of grief and other such states caused by that [body] shall not occur, as it would otherwise obscure his true nature. || 58 ||

Nor, through the firmness of cultivating the nature of one’s own Self as the Great Lord, can any defect such as incompleteness arise in the mind of this Knower; thus he demonstrates in the *Atigūḍhahṛdayagañja*:
For one who has fully developed the accumulation of the jewels of ultimate reality,
what misfortune could there be, and for whom, when the state of the Great Lord— realizing "I alone am He"— is attained? (59)
The heart itself is an exceedingly secret treasury,
its very nature being the place of rest for the true essence of all ultimate reality.

The treasury: therein, that supreme reality which has been taught by the true guru, which is rooted in the most intense and profound confidence, and whose essential nature is the knowledge of one's own Self—that alone is the "accumulation of jewels" because it is the cause of all manifestations, like a hoard of gems; for that reason, [one realizes] "I am indeed That."

When that state of Maheśvara— which is manifest as "I am all this," characterized by rest in the full supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*), and which constitutes the sovereignty of the self-luminous nature of one's own Self even for the embodied being— is present,
what indeed could be a wretched misfortune or a state of poverty, or any artificial condition characterized by such?

There would be an excellence such as sovereign power (*vibhūti*) and so forth. For all objects have appearance as their essence; at the very moment they appear, they are for the yogi identical with his own self. Being thus, how could they be capable of superiority or inferiority?
Thus, no such thing as poverty or the like would exist. Or for whom? That is to say, who could be the locus of this misfortune?
Indeed, let those who identify the self with the body and so forth be the ones who resort to this miserable state,
since they become masters through the attainment of that which is distinct from them and desirable.
"Devoid because of the loss of that"—

this refers to the knower whose ultimate reality is the reflective awareness of innate *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), who, as Maheśvara, thinks "I am everything," being inseparable from all that is to be sought; how could he [be devoid], since there is an absence of both the attainment and non-attainment of anything separate?

Would he not become a vessel for poverty and the like? Therefore, the qualifying attributes—*gañja* (treasury), *ratnasaṃcaya* (accumulation of jewels), and *īśvara* (lord)—have been established as denoting an unartificial meaning: that he is great, with the ultimate reality firmly rooted in his heart. || 59 ||
Now he describes the nature of liberation:
"For liberation there is no abode whatsoever, nor is there any going elsewhere."
Liberation is the piercing of the knot of ignorance and the manifestation of one's own power.
For liberation (mokṣa), which has as its essence the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā) and is absolute isolation (kaivalya),
there exists no abode whatsoever other than its own station.
Because there is no limitation by space, time, or form, for this very reason liberation is neither a departure nor a dissolution elsewhere into something distinct—

such as the view of the dualists who hold that liberation consists in the soul's ascent through the piercing of the centers (cakra) and its dissolution at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta). This alone is liberation.
As it has been said:
"What is the purpose of departing [from the body] when the existence of Śiva is all-pervasive?
Indeed, what is the purpose of departing when one is already non-limited within the supreme reality?"

Thus, there are many other such varieties of liberation imagined by other schools; however, were they to be elaborated here, they would lead to the fear of excessive prolixity, and so they are not detailed in this work. Since the stain of duality is present everywhere, the desire for liberation when there is no liberation is merely a semblance of liberation. What more need be said?

"What is the characteristic of liberation? To this he says, "Ignorance," and so forth. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is delusion (*moha*), characterized by the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) with respect to what is not-self—the body and so on—preceded by the conceit of non-self with respect to the Self; it is born from non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). That very [delusion] is called a "knot" (*granthi*) because, like a knot, it causes the contraction of one's full nature, which is characterized by one's own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
Bondage arises from the identification with the body and so forth [due to ignorance] regarding one's own pervasiveness and other qualities; its *bhitt* is the breaking or piercing of that [bondage].

Through the firm cultivation of the joy of one's own full and autonomous self-nature, there occurs the tearing asunder of the knot characterized by the identification with the body and so forth; for that reason, there arises through one's own powers—the attributes characterized by the autonomy of one's own self—the manifestation of those powers, which is the blossoming of the powers of one's own self. This alone is the unsurpassed liberation.

This is the intended meaning: just as space—which is endowed with qualities such as being innate, eternal, and all-pervasive—is nevertheless contracted by the confinement of walls such as jars, and for that very reason, that same [space] is called "jar-space" when it is endowed with qualities such as non-pervasiveness and appears as if distinct from [ordinary] space; so too, once again...

Upon the destruction of the contraction caused by the walls of a jar and so forth, that very same space within the jar would at that moment possess attributes such as all-pervasiveness; however, no new attribute whatsoever arises for it due to the destruction of the jar and so forth. It is exactly the same in this case.

Consciousness, contracted by the limitation produced through the identification with the body and so forth, is said to be "bound"; that same consciousness, however, when its own nature is manifested through the destruction of the bondage of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) such as the body, expands through the discernment of its own powers.

"Like one who is liberated"— thus, bondage and liberation have as their sole essence mere conceit from the perspective of a limited subject; however, in the ultimate sense, within the very reality of consciousness, nothing of this kind is possible.
Therefore, in liberation nothing new is accomplished; rather, one's own innate nature simply manifests. This very point is also stated in the *Viṣṇudharmas*:
"Just as by the making of a water-drawing well, the space within the water is not created [anew]."
Only that which exists is brought to manifestation; how could there be the arising of what is non-existent?
Just as when a leather bag is burst, the air within is no longer distinct from the surrounding air,
so too the self, once its bonds of merit and demerit are exhausted, is not separate from Brahman.
Thus [ends the verse]. 60.

Thus, one whose bond of ignorance has been destroyed, the man of knowledge (jñānī), though still maintaining a body for the sake of favoring others, is liberated— this is what [the text] indicates by the phrase "one who has split the knot of ignorance."
With doubts gone and delusion dispelled,
his merit and evil exhausted, he is liberated even while joined with a body. 61.

Even while connected with a body, one who knows their own true Self becomes liberated even while living, possessing fully blossomed power (*vikasvara-śakti*), due to the absence of identification with the body and other such things. [Objection: But surely, union with a physical form (*vigraha-yoga*) itself is bondage.

"How can he be liberated even while in connection with that [body]?"—to this he says "bhinna" and so forth. "Bhinna" means split open; he is one by whom the knot consisting of ignorance has been split, that is, the bondage consisting of the conceit of being the body and so forth, which arises from the manifestation of incompleteness. Likewise, "gatasaṃdehaḥ" (one whose doubt has vanished); for this very reason...

"Whose doubt is destroyed": he by whom delusion—the error consisting of duality—has been cast aside and suppressed through the attainment of supreme non-dual knowledge; such is the meaning. Through such constant cultivation, merits and demerits are exhausted and their latent impressions (saṃskāras) dissolve, due to the absence of the conceit that identifies the body with the self.

"Of whom [there are] dharma and adharma—he is of such a nature. By this, it is established that ignorance alone is bondage. And he for whom that [ignorance] is destroyed even while in union with a body is liberated at that very moment while still living; it is not the case that union with a body is bondage and its departure is liberation, but rather [he is liberated] prior to the fall of the body.
"Liberation," [it is said]. || 61 ||

For one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), even though the body— the cause of action— remains, his action, performed for the mere sake of maintaining the bodily existence and kindled by knowledge, does not [lead to rebirth].
Regarding the statement "it leads to that fruit," he provides the reasoning here:
just as a seed scorched by fire becomes incapable of sprouting.
Thus, action burnt by the fire of knowledge does not lead to rebirth.

Just as a grain of rice scorched by fire becomes incapable of producing a sprout and so forth, even while remaining amidst earth, water, and sunlight due to the deficiency of necessary conditions, in the same way,
karma that has been burnt by the fire of knowledge— that is, consumed by the radiance of supreme non-dual awareness— [becomes powerless].

"I alone manifest thus as the Self of the universe"— in this manner, through the abandonment of the conceit of identifying with the body and so forth, and by relinquishing the intellect that discriminates between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted,
whatever action— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is performed, its potency is burnt away; it does not bind the man of knowledge.
Immediately after the consumption of alms-food, it becomes the cause for the manifestation of a body that yields the fruit of birth,
just as a burnt seed [cannot produce] a sprout. Therefore, [it does not apply] to that which consists of the totality of the sense of "I" (sarvāhaṃbhāva).
An action performed by the power of consciousness (citiśakti) without the intention of fruit is not capable of granting further birth. || 62 ||
But how, then, can the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), which is likewise ever-expanding, come to possess a body? To this he replies:
