"Indeed, by virtue of its limited intellect, through the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a future body appropriate to its karma."
Constricted consciousness becomes such upon the destruction of this body. || 63 ||

Because, due to limited intelligence arising from non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), and through a resolve clouded by desire preceded by the latent impressions of identification with the body and so forth, one performs an action such as:
"I shall sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); may I be happy here and in the hereafter; may [evil] not..."
For an agent characterized by such latent impressions (vāsanā) as "May I never again experience suffering" or "By this action may I attain the station of Indra," [the result] conforms accordingly.
Karma; that future body, which is appropriate for the enjoyment of fruits corresponding to that karma— having attained full development through mental impressions—
is [the one] subsequent to the exhaustion of the authority over the body that experiences the fruits of *prārabdha* karma.

The future body— that mental impression (*bhāvanā*) regarding it, such as "May I attain sovereignty and so forth through this rite of the horse-sacrifice and the like"— is the mounting upon the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the desired fruit of the action;
by means of that impression of a future body appropriate to the action, this power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), though full in every respect, [becomes limited].

Perfumed by the *kārmamala*—which has as its root the *āṇava* and *māyīya* impurities—the all-pervasive [consciousness], though contracted like the space within a jar, becomes delimited by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body that experiences fruits according to its karma;
thus, upon the destruction of this body, it becomes so once again. Regarding this fruit of *prārabdha* karma...

The body is the enjoyer; when that body perishes due to the exhaustion of its experience—that destruction being death—then, upon the destruction of the body, that consciousness, possessing the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma that have arisen, becomes endowed with such a body as was the enjoyer of the fruit of those actions by which the fruit of previous karma had been acquired through that particular disposition (*āśaya*). It is by virtue of this [disposition] that [the consciousness assumes a new form].
Even consciousness (*cit*) would become a vessel for the enjoyment of heaven, hell, and so forth. Therefore, having become embodied,
because of a craving for limited results, whatever karma has been performed necessarily gives rise to a birth as an enjoyer of that fruit.

It prevails. However, as for that which has been accomplished by becoming bodiless through the nature of pure consciousness—that "I am all Brahman"—how could that lead to the birth of the pervasive power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), since it does not provide any soil for the sprouting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?
This is the intended meaning. || 63 ||
If it is argued that action accumulated through such selflessness leads the cognizer into saṃsāra,

then the true nature of the Self must be explained by which one would not be a transmigrator; thus, although this has already been established, he speaks again so that it may take root in the hearts of his disciples.
If, moreover, stainless awakening consists of a cognizer and an agent that has transcended all [limitations],
which is pervasive and neither set nor risen—
He whose form is light, whose resolve is truth. || 64 ||
The Lord is devoid of the divisions of space and time, eternal, immutable, perfectly complete.
The sole creator of the dissolution and emergence of the multitude of manifold powers. || 65 ||
One who perceives oneself as identical with Śiva, the supreme architect of the laws of creation and so forth—
how could such a person be a transmigrating being?
For that which is already spread out, whence or whither could there be any movement? || 66 ||

Furthermore, if a cognizer, whose heart has been pierced by the descent of supreme *śakti*, should cast aside the conceit of being a limited subject such as the body and awaken to his own self as consisting of Śiva, knowing it to be a single mass of consciousness and bliss, he—
How, and in what manner, could one who has fully realized his own nature as the Great Lord (maheśvara) be a transmigrating being (saṃsārī),

characterized by the habit of wandering through cyclic existence? He could not be so— this is the sense— because [his true nature] consists of the eightfold subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) composed of both consciousness and non-consciousness.

One transmigrates through connection with the impurity of karma (*kārmamala*). But how could he who is the singular embodiment of consciousness, consisting of Śiva, and whose veils of the *āṇavamala* and other impurities have been destroyed, be a transmigrating being?—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "What is wrong with [the claim] that he could be the singular embodiment of consciousness and yet also be a transmigrator? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Vitata" and so forth: for the cognizer who is "extended"—meaning whose space, time, and form are undivided—and who is full due to the exhaustion of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) created by himself preceded by the identification with the body and so on, how could there be any movement?
Because he is all-pervasive, what object exists apart from him that he might depend upon? From that [object],...

Could one who is separated elsewhere [from the Self] perform movement (*saṃsaraṇa*) or going (*gamana*) when [the body] is divided? For it is only for one who is delimited by the conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛtā*)—such as the body—that there can be the occurrence of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) such as the point of departure (*apādāna*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). But as for him who is a single mass of consciousness (*cidekaghana*)...
The knower, having become Brahman, is unlimited by space and time; for such a one, even the verbal expression "transmigration" would not exist.
How should he awaken to the Self as the form of Śiva? To this he says: "pure"—page 126—[and so forth].

"Awakening," and so forth: that from which the accumulation of impurities such as *āṇava* and the rest has departed; therefore, due to that very purity, it is "awakening," which is pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*). Likewise, it is that in which the previously mentioned absolute sovereignty of knowledge and action—which transcends all and is unsurpassed—is inherent. It is "extended" (*vitata*) because there is an absence of any limitation caused by space and the like.

Pervasive; likewise, he whose form—his very body—is that light of consciousness (*bodha-dīpti*) for whom there is neither setting nor rising, and thus no dissolution or emergence; furthermore, he whose intentions are true—that is, ultimate—and who wanders according to his own will, such that whatever he desires comes to pass exactly so: [he is] of such a nature. And likewise...

It is devoid of considerations of direction, time, and form; because it possesses the qualities of pervasiveness and eternity, it is therefore fixed (*dhruva*), immutably stable (*kūṭastha*), and imperishable (*avyaya*). Likewise, it is the Lord (*īśvara*), being independent.
Furthermore, it is perfectly full and utterly free from desire. Following that, [there are] many more...

He is independent in the process of the dissolution and origination of the vast multitude of powers— such as those of jars, cloths, and so forth— which arise from the mass of sounds and are presided over by the powers of Brahmā and others; furthermore, he is the creator, the supreme architect, highly skilled and proficient in the methods of creation and the rest.
Knowing one's own Self as the Great Lord (Maheśvara), completely full in every respect through such qualifying attributes as these, whatever [little]...
Acting thus, with the seeds of karma burnt away, he no longer partakes in saṃsāra; he becomes liberated even while living—this is the sense. || 64 || 65 || 66 ||

Thus, demonstrating that even an action performed by a knower— who, through the attainment of self-reflection, has dissolved all desire for the fruits of karma— does not lead to further results, he states a worldly analogy established by his own experience:
Thus, it is established even by reasoning that the action of one who possesses knowledge is not fruitful;
for [the thought] "this is not mine, but rather his"—
Thus, because of its firmness, there is no fruit in the world [from mere words]. || 67 ||

I alone am the mass of consciousness, autonomous, performing all actions as the innermost essence of all subjects; nor am I the agent, for [agency belongs to] the supreme Lord— page 128— [who is the source].

"The power of absolute freedom acts in this way"— what does this have to do with me, who am of the nature of pure consciousness? For the knowing subject who knows the nature of his own self as explained by these logical arguments and proofs whose essential nature was previously established, [the conclusion holds] in both ways.

Because of the absence of the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth, action that is established as being devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—even if performed—is not fruitful; it is not joined with a result. For such a knower of the Self, since there is an absence of artificiality in both ways as previously explained, where could even performed action find a connection with a result?
How could it act? Since the basis consisting of the nature of the conceit of being an agent (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth is absent, [it acts] nowhere at all—this is the sense.
For an agent, the firm establishment of the conceit of possessing the fruit of an action performed is precisely that basis;
however, for the knower (*jñānin*), due to the absence of such conceit, the action is exhausted within its own very form and does not [result] in a fruit.
"It is connected"—thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: "In what way is it that one is joined with the fruit of action solely through conceit?
To this he says: "Not even 'this is mine,'" and so forth. And this is observed, not something unprecedented: namely, that even this action such as sacrifice is not "mine."
However,
for any such purposeful sacrificer,

even though ritual acts such as sacrifice have been performed with this understanding, they do not [bear fruit] in this world because of the desire for payment and the absence of pride regarding the result; for that reason, it is so.

Action is considered to be endowed with a fruit belonging to the next world; for instance, according to the principle that "the officiating priests sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*) while "the patron sacrifices" (*yajate yajamānaḥ*), even though the sacrificial rite is performed by the sacrificing priests themselves,
this sacrificial act such as the Aśvamedha belongs to us [the priests] in no way, but rather to the one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*).

"O meritorious one! We, it seems, are here merely seeking the fixed wages for our sacrificial work; there are none here who, like the patron (*yajamāna*), partake of the fruits such as heaven resulting from this rite. Thus, because they lack any conceit regarding the fruits of action, they do not [suffer] themselves.

Even though the ritual action has been performed, it is joined with its fruit, such as heaven, for the patron (*yajamāna*); for the patron, while not performing the sacrificial act there himself and merely looking toward the work accomplished by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [thinks]: "This sacrificial act, such as the Aśvamedha, is mine; these priests are performing the rite with my wealth."

Thinking, "Since these [actions] have already begun, the fruit such as heaven will necessarily accrue to me after the fall of the body," it is just as for one who does not act [out of this conviction].

Because of the firmness of the conceit regarding the fruit of the action desired, that action of his is joined with its fruit. For this very reason, when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent, the *ātmanepada* ending is used—as in "the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) sacrifices" (*yajate*)—referring to the agent who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*); but when the fruit is not intended for the agent, the *parasmaipada* ending is used—as in "the officiating priests (*yājaka*) sacrifice" (*yajanti*). Such is the distinction.

The majesty of the freedom of conceptualization (*vikalpa-svātantrya*) is difficult to surpass: that even an action performed by oneself is not joined with its fruit due to the absence of the conceit of agency regarding that fruit, whereas an action performed by others may be joined with its fruit through the firmness of the conceit "this is mine. Therefore, [an action] being performed is like the activity of a priest (*ṛtvij*).
Because the yogin lacks the conceit of being the agent of action, that [action] would not bear fruit—thus [ends the verse]. || 67 ||

Thus, one whose intellect has abandoned the stain of conceptualizing what is to be rejected or accepted in all actions becomes an illumined knower— thus he says: "In this way, all mental constructs..."
Awakened by the wind of meditative cultivation,
one becomes composed of light while offering oblations into the blazing light of the Self. 68.

In the manner thus explained, that cultivation which consists of the firm establishment of self-awareness (*vimarśa*) within oneself— namely, "I alone am the Great Lord of Consciousness; I manifest in this way at all times and in every respect"— is itself, as it gradually expands like the wind (*samīraṇa*), by means of that [cultivation], the Knower.
Awakened like a fire covered in ashes that is rekindled by the wind, I perceive all conceptual constructions:
"I am a bound beast, fettered by the bonds of karma, embodied in this form; these are my son, wife, and so forth;
by this action, heaven or hell will come to pass"—all such imaginings are merely myself. This is I.

Offering everything— rendered as a residue of reflective awareness— into the blazing fire of the light of the Self, which consists of the essence of the wonder of supreme I-consciousness, and thus surrendering it by entering into the nature of non-conceptual consciousness,
he becomes composed of that light.

Because the fuel of the conceptualization of the object to be burned is exhausted, the fire of consciousness itself becomes the form of the burner; that which remains is this [consciousness] whose sole body is the supreme subject—this is the meaning. || 68 ||
In the manner thus explained, how does one who is devoted to the practice of the yoga of superior knowledge pass the time with his remaining life? To this he says:
"Eating whatever [it may be]."
Clad in whatever he may have, peaceful,
dwelling wherever he may be, he whose self is the soul of all beings is liberated. 69.

Eating whatever edible object happens to fall before him, he remains in a state of wonder, not according to fixed rules, because he is devoid of the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted— such as thinking, "this is pure," "this is impure," "this is coarse food," or "this is sweet food."
Gathering whatever comes to him without effort— even that— being thus clothed by means of a rag, a hide, bark, or cotton cloth and so forth, or even by divine garments.

"He is covered"—thus, because there is neither increase nor decrease in either case, having become one who seeks the purposeful activity of covering the body, he neither hates anything nor praises it.
How is this so? Because he is peaceful, having transcended the conceptual constructions of pleasure, pain, and the like. Likewise:

"Residing anywhere whatsoever" means: in whatever kind of place it may be, seeking only one's own shelter; neither is a field, a temple, a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or the like to be accepted because of its purity, nor is a cremation ground, the dwelling of a dog-eater (*śvapaca*), or the like to be avoided because of its impurity.

It may be that he dwells in whatever state happens upon him without effort, because he is free from the stain of conceptualizing purity and impurity. Regarding the phrase "he is liberated": even while thus spending his time through the persistence of residual karma, having set out for the sake of favoring others, he is liberated and becomes Supreme Śiva. Thus it has been said.
And:
covered with whatever [is available], fed with whatever [is available]— page 134— [he remains thus].
The gods know him as a Brahmin who sleeps wherever he may happen to be.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Mokṣadharma*,
there is food to be chewed, eaten, and drunk with non-fixed results,
distinguished by injunctions and distributed according to place and time.
I, pure, practice this Ājagara vow, which brings happiness to the heart and is not pursued by the miserly.
Thus [it is asked]: "How can one who acts even in this way be liberated himself as a man of knowledge? To this he says: "The Self of all beings.
Because the man of knowledge is the Self of all beings—the Self of all beings and all beings are his Self—therefore nothing exists as a cause of bondage; everything [is the Self].
This leads to his liberation—thus [it is said]. || 69 ||
Nor is it the case that for one who is thus [realized], free from conceit, and performing whatever action may arise, there can be the production of merit or demerit; so he says:
[Page 135]
One who knows the ultimate truth does not [accumulate] even hundreds of thousands of horse-sacrifices or hundreds of thousands of killings of Brahmins through meritorious deeds.
And being stainless, he is not touched by sins. || 70 ||
He who thus knows the ultimate truth, who understands the true nature of his own self as the Great Lord (Maheśvara),
performs innumerable sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, and Aptoryāma—
not out of desire for fruits or pride, but simply by regarding them as duties to be performed.
Whether one performs prescribed actions for the sake of play, or whether one commits unprescribed great sins such as killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, or theft due to negligence—
even because of being bodiless— in both cases, there is an absence of the conceit of "I" and "mine."

The will of the Supreme Lord alone unfolds in this manner; with the realization that "what concern is this of mine," that man of knowledge is touched neither by meritorious deeds with their auspicious fruits, nor by sins with their inauspicious results.

"It is being made impure"—how so? To this he says: "It is stainless" (*vimala*). For its *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* impurities—the causes of transmigratory existence—have departed and been destroyed. Thus, for the impure cognizer (*pramātṛ*), there exists the state of conceiving "self" and "mine" by virtue of having a fragmented sense of selfhood regarding the body and other such things.

By whomsoever there might be an accumulation of merit and demerit due to the wickedness of the conceit "this action of mine is auspicious" or "this [action] is inauspicious"— for one from whom the accumulation of the fruits of action,
which is the cause of the notion of "mine" and a heap of impurities, has departed, how could there be [such a thing] due to the absence of conceit?
The touch of merit and demerit: as it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā,
"He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound."
Thus [ends the verse]. 70.
Reflecting upon the constant conduct of such a knower, he says:
"One who is entirely free from pride, joy, anger, passion, despondency, fear, greed, and delusion."
Free from the utterance of *stotra* and *vaṣaṭ*,
he should wander like one who is dull-witted, his mind beyond dispute.
Intoxication (*mada*) is the conceit of being an embodied subject; joy (*harṣa*) is the delight arising from the acquisition of what was not previously obtained;
anger (*kopa*) is wrath; passion (*manmatha*) is the longing for sexual enjoyment; and despondency (*viṣāda*) arises from separation from the beloved.
Delusion, fear of enemies or of lions, tigers, and the like, greed, miserliness,

and the delusion consisting of the sense of "I" and "mine" toward living beings— all these reflections arising from the impressions of the body, even when they occur intermittently, he completely abandons by realizing, "I am Brahman."

By entering into the nature of non-conceptual consciousness, he brings [all things] to a state where they remain as nothing but the self-reflection of his own Self. Thus, he who has emerged from hymns and *vaṣaṭ*-calls— since there is no object of praise distinct from him— has no need for hymns and the like, nor does he rely on mantras such as *vaṣaṭ*.
Because of the absence of any distinct deity for one who is [already] divided; he would merely wander like an insentient being, his mind devoid of discourse.

Due to his fullness and lack of desire, he is like a madman regarding what ought to be done—whether in the form of scriptural action established by valid means of knowledge, or in the true nature of the object of knowledge together with other knowers—as to whether "this is appropriate" or "this is not."
"No"— thus, one whose intellect is excluded from deliberation [does not require instruction];
nor does he require instruction for himself, or for the sake of instructing others regarding the object of knowledge.

He presents [this view]: having become for the most part subdued, one should simply wander about for the sake of play while perceiving everything as Brahman; thus he is described as being like an insentient object. || 71 ||

Even though the group beginning with pride (*mada*) is thus avoided, one might ask: "Why is the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) not touched by these, just as we are, while he still possesses a body? To this, he states the reason:
"This [group] beginning with pride and exhilaration (*harṣa*..."
The sense of "group" arises from the delusion of differentiation;
therefore, how indeed could the realization of the non-dual Self be touched by it? (72)
Immediately following the commentary on the *Kārikās*, this section on "Intoxication" (*mada*) and so forth begins with the words: "This [intoxication] arises from the delusion of differentiation.

This delusion of differentiation, which consists of the notions of "self" and "mine," is the manifestation of incompleteness; from that, it originates for the bound subjects (*paśu-pramātṛs*) through the error of duality, arising as the state of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted. Furthermore, that which...
The supreme realization of the non-dual Self is "I am all, I am Brahman.
Such a person of exalted knowledge is like the sky; how indeed could he be affected by that group beginning with pride?
In what manner could it be defiled? For how could one thing ever impart its own nature to another that is distinct from it?

Since the group beginning with "I" (the ego) is perceived as being of the nature of Brahman, how could it be a source of opposition for the knower who has become Brahman and belongs to the same genus? Thus [ends the verse]. || 72 ||
Even the category of external praise and oblation is based solely on duality and is not sufficient for his satisfaction;
thus he says:
"Whether that which is to be praised or that which is to be offered..."
There is nothing whatsoever separate from him;
he is satisfied by hymns and the like,
yet he is liberated, being free from prostrations and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
For the knower whose nature is non-dual awareness, there is nothing whatsoever distinct from that state— neither any form of deity to be praised, nor anything to be offered as an oblation.

There exists a distinct form— that which is praised or offered in sacrifice— and yet that knower of the Self does not attain satisfaction through such acts as praise performed with the notion that they are "to be done. For,
by virtue of his enjoyment of the realization of non-duality, he consists of eternal bliss and thus does not value artificial pleasure.
Therefore, he who has emerged from the *namas* and *vaṣaṭ* [offerings] is indeed the one liberated and praised thus in the Vedāntas;
nor does he have any need for a separate temple, for his own body alone is the abode of the deity of the Self or the locus of consciousness, and nothing else— thus, it is not separate.
"This is his temple," he said,
"consisting of the thirty-six principles, filled with windows formed by the arrangement of its body."
Then, his own body or another, such as a jar and so forth, is his temple. (74)
For that knower, his own body or even the body of another is the temple of the deity,
because it serves as the substratum for the enjoyment of the deity who is one's own Self. As for external temples, such as those on Mount Meru, they are [merely] then...

When the preceptor has conceived [the disciple] as having become a temple of the deity through the pervasion of his own body— which consists of the reckoning of the thirty-six principles— then even an external deity present therein, being embraced by the density of consciousness through the pervasion of his own self, becomes a deity there; otherwise, both of these would be insentient.
How could that which is like a mere fragment of stone uplift devotees or lead those who have died to states such as *sāmīpya* (proximity) and so forth?

Thus, in its primary sense, the body is the temple of the deity because it is the locus of consciousness; the deity is one's own Self (*svātmā*) residing within it. Therefore, for one who is fully awakened, the body itself is the temple of the deity. Of what kind is it?

What is that? He says: "the thirty-six principles" (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*). The external [temple] is conceived through the pervasion of the thirty-six principles; however, the supreme temple of the body is directly filled and nourished by the thirty-six principles. In an external temple there is the arrangement of windows, but this—
"Filled with the windows of the arrangement of the body": "arrangement" (*racanā*) refers to the sequence of the doors of the sense organs within the "body" (*vigraha*); that very [sequence] is...
[page 142]
It is filled and undiminished by that conceptualization of *tāmora* (the darkness of ignorance);

thus, it is like an external temple. It is not only the body that is a temple of the Divine on the grounds that it is the locus of consciousness; rather, whatever is presided over by consciousness—all of that is its temple.

Thus he says: "or the jar and so forth. This pentad of objects, characterized by the jar and the rest, which is of the nature of the object of enjoyment, is presided over by consciousness through the doors of the eyes and other senses;
indeed, the enjoyer himself always exists everywhere in the form of the enjoyed. (3.2)

Thus, according to the perspective of the teachings of the *Spanda-śāstra*, everything consists of consciousness alone. For the Knower, the entire universe—beginning with jars and so forth—is a "body of existence" (*bhāva-śarīra*), just like the physical body of living beings. Considering it thus, even that [universe] is non-different from himself, like his own body;
it is the "abode of the God," the house of the Great Lord who is one's own Self, the independent and playful Deity.
The substratum of the object of enjoyment—thus [ends the section]. || 74 ||

It is said that in an external temple, a devotee is seen intent on worshipping the deity after first bringing flowers and other offerings; but what does the Knower do while presiding over the temple of the body? To this, he says: page 143 [The text continues: "He who, having first brought the flowers of the senses and the like, is intent on worshipping the deity of consciousness within the temple of the body—he is truly a knower. Thus he speaks.
And there, [one should worship] the deity Paramātma-mahābhairava-Śiva together with his own Śakti,
which is pure through the self-reflection (ātmāmarśana) [of consciousness].
He remains worshipping with material offerings. || 75 ||

In that temple of one's own body, the supreme yogin is the Self characterized by consciousness, which is the highest and transcends all; He alone is Bhairava because of His proficiency in dissolving the enjoyment of all objects such as sound and the rest, and because of His sustaining (bharaṇa)— .
He whose nature is the vomiting of [all] sounds—that very one is the deity Śiva, the God who is the form of supreme bliss.
Constantly worshipping her, he should manifest himself while satiating her according to the sequence to be described.
Now, one might ask: "An external deity is accompanied by a retinue; why should he worship this [deity] as being accompanied by a retinue?"

Thus he says, "endowed with her own powers" (*svaśaktiyutām*). Her own powers (*svāḥ śaktayaḥ*) are the powers of the instruments, such as the eyes and so forth, which consist of the radiance of consciousness and are of the nature of the manifestations of the powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action.
[He dwells] surrounded on all sides by those [energies]. With what does he remain engaged in worship? To this he says:
"The self-reflection," and so forth. This reflection that "all this is indeed one's own self" (svātmaiva idaṃ sarvam) is...

The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by resting in the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), which consists of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatā*) of all objects, results in the complete destruction of the stain of the impurity of duality; thereby, the fivefold objects such as sound and so forth— which serve as the materials for worship— become pure through the removal of their insentience (*jāḍya*).

"They are purified by those substances which are stainless due to the absence of self-grasping"—this is the intended meaning. The point is this: the man of knowledge (jñānin), having abandoned the stain of the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, gathers the fivefold objects such as sound—which present themselves effortlessly—by means of the goddesses who are the senses (the auditory organ and so forth), and while experiencing internal wonder, [realizes] non-difference from his own Self.

He brings about this state—thus, at the time of incessantly appropriating each respective object, that internal wonder which is the flashing forth of the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness) is itself the worship of one’s own self as the deity. For this very reason, objects such as sound and the rest are the implements of worship; therefore, for one who possesses focused attention, at the time of perceiving objects—

"One should become a worshiper of one's own self as the deity at every moment"— this is what those who know the secret have declared. Rājānaka Rāma has composed this very point by way of praise, as follows:
That [world] which is satiated by your powers, such as the Taijasī and others, who are intent on offering the oblation of the world’s very being brought forth by their ever-unrestrained exertion—
that [world] is offered within this body, a dwelling in a cremation ground, mired in a heap of flesh, blood, fat, and bones.
Behold my terrifying form, that of a hero wandering through the night of worldly existence.
Thus [ends the verse]. 75.
"At the conclusion of the worship, there must be an oblation into the fire"—how is this possible for one who possesses knowledge? To this he says:
"For one who offers the great mass of seeds consisting of the distinctions between external and internal conceptualization..."
In the intensely blazing fire of his consciousness, the oblation occurs without effort. || 76 ||
For such a person, who worships his own self as the deity, within the fire of consciousness— which is exceedingly radiant and shines with the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā)—
[page 146]

Without effort, and apart from the hardship of procuring sesame, clarified butter, fuel, and so forth, the *homa*—the satiation of the fire—is accomplished. Doing what? To this he says: "externally and internally," and so on.

Externally, regarding objects of knowledge such as blue and the like, there is the conceptualization of self and other subjects; and internally, regarding that which is grasped, such as pleasure and the like...

The differentiation between the external and internal— the subject and the object— consisting of the nature of the functions of determination, conceptualization, and self-conceit, is precisely this manifoldness that serves as the "great seed" from which the subject and object arise; for it is that very differentiation, consisting of conceptual construction, which constitutes the seed of duality.

A "heap" (*nicaya*) is a collection because of its endlessness; for one who offers that heap—by means of the supreme non-dual vision, through entering the nature of non-conceptual consciousness, and by sacrificing it into the fire of one's own Self—this is the intended meaning: since the yogin, whose self is the Supreme Brahman, lacks the conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛ*) such as the body and so forth, [that which arises]...

That very state, established by its own inherent nature (*svarasasiddha*), wherein the conceptualization of self and other, as well as subject and object, has completely ceased—that alone is the unartificial *homa*.
As the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīravāmanaka said:
"Wherein the forest of duality is the fuel, and death itself is the great sacrificial animal."
With that supramundane sacrifice, we worship eternally.
Thus [ends the verse] 76.
Thus, he speaks of the meditation of such a sacrificer: "Furthermore, this Blessed One has meditations that do not set, for they take on various forms."
He creates that very meditation,
which possesses the nature of truth as if inscribed by his own volition.
There is a cessation of a contemplated form when that form, having been fixed in its specific aspect, departs from the mental activity to another;
however, this meditation is never-setting, because even this Blessed One,
the infinite Maheśvara whose nature is his own self, [perceives] those [objects] through the sovereignty of conceptualization which is the very essence of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

It incessantly creates diverse forms and delineates various conceptualized objects and shapes upon the mirror of the intellect; that alone is its meditation and contemplation, which is devoid of rising and setting, and nothing other than this exists. However, in the case of another [form], namely a specific deity—

There would be no restriction [to specific forms] through the conceptualization of various faces and limbs; for one who knows that every mental activity is a sprout of the expansion of the Supreme Power (parāśakti), all this remains undivided.

It has become the Supreme Goddess. Likewise, it is that meditation which, though drawn by the mind through volition and painted upon the wall of consciousness, possesses the nature of reality—that is, ultimate truth. Thus, all this which is manifest, though inscribed by conceptual construction and consisting of mental activity, [is of that nature].
Reality is not distinct from manifestation, because consciousness pervades everything— thus it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda-śāstra*:
"Wherever the mind goes, one should fix [the awareness] right there."
Having moved, where will you go, since everything consists of auspiciousness?

Thus it is said; likewise, in the Śaivopaniṣad: "O beloved, wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally—therein lies the state of Śiva; because of its all-pervasiveness, where could it go?"
Thus, for this reason, this meditation of the yogin arises spontaneously— so it is said. || 77 ||
And what should his recitation (*japa*) be like? To this he says:
"The entire series of worlds, the conceptualization of the sequence of principles (*tattva*), and likewise the group of sense organs."
That which he transforms within his inner consciousness is declared to be his recitation (japa). || 78 ||

The reflective awareness of the Supreme I-ness (*parāhaṃtā*) toward the universe at every moment, through non-differentiation, according to the sequence that will be explained—this is declared to be its *japa* (recitation); it is described as being uncreated (*akṛtrima*).
What is this? He says: "the entire series of worlds."
The entire series of two hundred and forty walls situated within the collection of thirty-six principles (*tattva*), as well as the conceptualization of the sequence of principles— that is,
the determination of the sequence of principles known as *Ātman*, *Vidyā*, and *Śiva*— and furthermore, the group of sense organs (*akṣagaṇa*).
Thus,
[he perceives] the collection of the senses, which consists of the internal and external organs— within, that is,
in his own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), which serves as the string for the beads of the middle vital energy (*madhyamaprāṇaśakti*).

By means of the sequence of the flow of *nāda* and *bindu*, that which revolves like a waterwheel (*araghaṭṭa-ghaṭīyantra*)—through the sequence of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal of every projection of breath (*prāṇa*)—causes all this to revolve within its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), and at every moment perceives it as the essence of *nāda*; such is the meaning. That very [reality]...

His recitation (*japa*) is unartificial, characterized by resting in the fullness of *ahantā* (I-consciousness). This is the intended meaning: recitation is indeed the utterance of the mantra—the signifier—of the deity who is the signified;
and that [utterance] is to be counted by means of a rosary (*akṣamālā*) through the sequence of turning the beads, which is pervaded by the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*).

For the supreme non-dual yogi, however, his own vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*), which serves as the thread, vibrating through the sequence of the flow within the central breath (*madhyama-prāṇa*) and arising spontaneously by its own essence, is called the "natural rosary" (*sahajā akṣamālā*) because it encompasses all the senses. For all this that is to be expressed consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).

The universe, being established solely within the power of *prāṇa*, [is perceived] through the sequence of arising and passing away with every movement of the breath; thus, the Blessed Lady, whose nature is supreme (*parā*), assumes the form of *prāṇa*.
Reflecting upon every vibration of the breath, the attentive yogin accomplishes uncontrived recitation (*japa*).
In this regard, the number of recitations for a day and night is twenty-one thousand six hundred.
The recitation of the Goddess has been taught; it is easily attained, yet difficult for the dull-witted to achieve.

Thus it is said in the Śaiva Upaniṣad; and in the Śivasūtras: "The story [of Śiva] is the recitation" (Sūtra 3.27). In this way, this [teaching] is within the range of only those who possess devotion and whose feet are worthy of worship—thus [ends the section]. || 78 ||
"This is his vow"— thus he says—
referring to everything that one sees with the vision of the *samaya* and whatever consciousness one perceives.
She is devoted to all cremation grounds and is adorned with the arrangement of a corpse and a khaṭvāṅga staff. || 79 ||
The skull-bowl in his own hand, filled with the essence of the nectar of the universe, is the fragment of the knowable.
And because it causes [the self] to relish [the truth], this vow of his is both very difficult to attain and easily attained. || 80 ||

Thus, that which is about to be described is precisely this vow (*vrata*) of the wise one—a discipline (*niyama*) for the propitiation of the deity who is one's own Self. Of what nature is it? To this he says: "It is both very difficult to attain and easy to attain. It is very difficult to attain because it is achieved only with great effort through the destruction of nescience (*akhyāti*).
It is obtained through the grace of the Supreme Lord in the form of the abandonment of all other means; therefore, it is very difficult to attain.

Likewise, it is easily attained because it is obtained without the hardship of accepting external ornaments such as bones and ashes, or the observance of dietary restrictions and the like; therefore, it is also easy to attain. What is that vow? To this he says: "Everything," and so forth.

Whatever appears here as this entire manifold manifestation of difference, through the cultivation of reasoning, scripture, and experience, I shine as this one whole by means of the vision of non-duality.
Thus he contemplates, as it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"One whose self is disciplined by yoga, who sees with equal vision everywhere, beholds the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self" (6.29).
And so forth. Thus, the very firmness of the cognition of non-duality is the *vrata*.

Furthermore, that which considers consciousness to be intent upon the cremation ground of the universe (*viśva-śmaśāna*) is also the *vrata*. For example, [considering] the universe, which has the nature of the grasped and the grasper...

Because it is occupied by hundreds of corpses consisting of insentient objects such as jars and bodies, that very place is a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), a burial ground (*pitṛvana*); for since the one Blessed Consciousness alone is non-insentient, everything else manifested by Her is insentient and thus comparable to a corpse. Therefore, [the world] is a cremation ground for the universe.

Similarity: In that universal cremation ground, which is utterly terrifying due to the birth and death of all things, he—being a practitioner (*vratī*) who indeed dwells in a cremation ground—considers and perceives consciousness (*saṃvid*) as residing in its midst, having become entirely intent upon it. Furthermore, this [practitioner]...

The extraordinary practitioner (*alaukiko vratī*), realizing everywhere that "I alone am the ultimate reality of the single state of consciousness," [remains so] together with insentient beings such as the animal-like subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) such as jars, which occupy the status of the "other."

Acting like one mad, he dwells upon this ground of saṃsāra— which is terrifying by nature because it is a cremation ground due to the destruction of all subjects and objects of knowledge— while performing his play.
Furthermore, he regards consciousness as being fashioned by the conceptualization of a corpse and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

The "vigraha" is the body; that very thing constitutes the arrangement of the *khaṭvāṅga* (the skull-topped staff), which is the ritual of the skeleton. Indeed, for the yogin—who, through the destruction of the stubborn grasp of the conceit of being the subject (*pramātṛ*) of his own body, considers his own Self to be transcendent of the body—the body, reduced to a mere residual impression, is essentially like a corpse. Thus it is said.

For one who perceives his own body as nothing but the construction of a skeleton-seal (*kaṅkālamudrā*), it is sealed—that is, marked—as the substratum of objects of enjoyment by that [seal]. Indeed, for a practitioner of the Hero’s Vow (*vīravratī*) situated in a cremation ground, it is auspicious to be marked by the skull-topped staff seal (*khaṭvāṅgamudrā*); therefore, even his own body belongs to this [practitioner] whose form is his own self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*).
For one who perceives that which is divided by its state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*), that very [perception] is the *khaṭvāṅga* mudrā; this too is his vow.
Likewise, he tastes the skull-cup (*kapāla*) which is a fragment of the object of knowledge.
He chews; and that which consists of the fivefold objects of sense such as sound and so forth— this entire nature of the object of enjoyment,

which is limited by its status as an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and an effect (*kārya*), and is thus fragmentary like a broken potsherd— that very thing he relishes as a *kapāla*, a piece of the skull or a fragment of bone.
Through the process of extracting the essence and resting in full identity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), one experiences wonder—this too is a vow.
Indeed, the practitioner of the vow tastes the "heroic drink" (*vīrapāna*) situated in the skull; thus he says, "the universal flavor" (*viśvarasa*).
That which is the essential portion within the skull-fragment, which consists of the fivefold objects of perception such as sound and so forth throughout the universe—[that is what is tasted].

That very portion consisting of the nectar of relish (carvaṇāmṛta), because it bestows supreme bliss, is the "essence-liquor" (rasāsava)—the finest of drinks; by that [drink], it is "full," meaning completely filled. This is what is meant: that part of the universe which is like the hard crust or shell, serving as the vessel, is itself the skull-cup (kapāla); [the nectar] resides within it.

The essential portion, which is capable of producing wonder because it bestows delight, is the "drink"—thus [it is said]. As for the skull, it resides in the hand of the practitioner; hence he says "in his own hand" (*nijakaragam*). His own hands (*nijāḥ karāḥ*) are the rays of consciousness whose nature consists of the goddesses of the senses, such as sight and so forth; in them, that [essence] exists as an object of enjoyment.

The fragment of the object becomes the state of being an object— this is our own experience; just as a drink is drunk from a skull-cup held in the hand, so too is the wine of the essence of the universe [drunk] from the skull-cup of the fragment of the object.
The yogi, having withdrawn [the objects] by means of the hands that are the cognitions of the eyes and other senses, tastes them. This is the intended meaning:

the yogi always, as each of the five objects arises, has them withdrawn by the goddesses of the senses and, through this method, maintains an uninterrupted rest in his own Bhairava-consciousness until the final moment.

He carries out exactly what has been taught through the vision of non-duality—this alone is the vow of one who has cultivated the lotus feet of a true guru; anything other than this is merely the emaciation of the body.
Summarizing what has been previously established, he states the excellence of this instruction:
"Having realized that which is devoid of birth and destruction, known as the Supreme Lord of Ultimate Reality..."
Because the state of being a perceiver is no longer manifest,
he remains as he pleases, having accomplished all that was to be done.
Thus, in the manner just described, having realized within one's own self that secret reality called Paramārthamaheśvara— the authentic Maheśvara— what has been established...

Having correctly experienced it through firm practice—of what nature? He says: "devoid of birth and destruction," meaning that once this is attained, there shall be no more arising or death. "He remains as he pleases, having accomplished all that was to be done" means that having attained this, the yogi, because there is no further duty remaining and having achieved the supreme human goal (*parapuruṣārtha*), remains as he wishes.

Without transgressing his own will, he remains maintaining his body through his sovereignty like the whirling of a wheel, passing the time. How so? It is said: "because of the manifestation of the state of being the perceiver. Through the cultivation of this secret, there is manifestation as the experiencer in all states.
"From that, there is throbbing"—this means that even while residing in the body, one is composed of full bliss. || 81 ||

Thus, he states that there is no restriction regarding the qualified practitioner, meaning that whoever among the living recognizes their own self in this way would become identical with that [divine] form.
Thus described as all-pervading, the self of all, with diversity shaken off,
and consisting of incomparable supreme bliss—
He who knows it becomes identical with it. || 82 ||

In this manner— that is, by the method described— Śiva, who is all-pervasive and a single compact mass of uninterrupted consciousness and bliss, has been declared; he who knows Him— whoever among living beings understands Him through the process of cultivating reasoning, scripture, and personal experience— he, having abandoned all contraction, becomes identical with Him and is Śiva himself.
It may be so. In this regard, there is no restriction regarding those qualified for the knowledge of one’s own Self;

for whoever—be they even animals tainted by the defects of birth, death, and so forth—all become identical with Him through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of their own Self as the Great Lord. This is the sense of the word "whoever" (*ye*).

[The word] *parāmarśaḥ* [is used]. And of what kind? "The self of all" (*sarvātmānam*). That which is the self of all subjects and objects of knowledge, or that whose self is all subjects and objects of knowledge—that is, transcendent to all.

"Consisting of all"—this is the meaning. For this very reason, it is that by which multiplicity—the endlessness of differentiation—is shaken off and surpassed, because it manifests at all times and in all places as the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Thus...
One who knows one's own self as being thus—characterized by such a supreme bliss which is incomparable due to the absence of desire and devoid of qualifiers—would be of the nature of Śiva. || 82 ||

Thus, having realized his own self as the Great Lord, one might wonder: "Upon the exhaustion of the authority over his own body, where would he cast off the body, or what state would he go to?"—it is to dispel such doubts that [the scripture] says:
"Whether at a sacred pilgrimage site or in the house of an outcaste."
Even one whose memory has failed, by abandoning the body,
is liberated at the very moment of knowledge and, with sorrow destroyed, attains absolute isolation (kaivalya).

Thus, one who has thoroughly cultivated their own true nature— the man of knowledge (jñānī)— whose heart is firmly consoled by the vision of supreme non-duality, [realizing] that "all this is the sovereign freedom of the light of one's own Self," [approaches] the sacred ford (tīrtha) such as Prayāga, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and so forth.
Whether casting off the body in a place of great merit, or else in the abode of a dog-cooker— a dwelling characterized as that of an outcaste, which is most sinful— in both ways.
Even though he is free from the afflictions of acceptance and rejection, he attains liberation (*kaivalya*) solely through self-knowledge upon the dissolution of the body;

that is to say, he reaches a state of absolute oneness (*kevalatā*)—which is distinct from the entire range of causes and effects beginning with *pradhāna*—consisting of a single mass of pure consciousness (*cidānanda*), transcending the fourth state (*turyātīta*). For this reason, his...

For one who perceives this entire universe as full of his own self, governed by the Supreme Lord through an impartial vision, there is no distinction between the field (*kṣetra*) and the non-field; for this very reason, he is one by whom sorrow—arising from conceptual constructions and doubts—is destroyed or cast aside. As it has been said:
In the Himavat, at Gaṅgādvāra, in Vārāṇasī, in Kuru, or at Prayāga;
or in the house of a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste.
For those who know the principle of Śiva, death is the same [for all].
Thus, in the *Śrī-nirvāṇayogottara*: "Nor is there any need for mindfulness at the moment of the body's fall"—so he says: "Even one whose memory has perished...
[page 161]

Thus [it is said]. Let alone the recollection—this is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also). Or rather, at the time of abandoning the body, that knower may have his memory lost due to being overwhelmed by the wind, bile, and phlegm arising from that [body], and thus, being like wood or stone, devoid of self-awareness, he becomes helpless regarding the physical frame.

Even though he abandons [the body], nevertheless, one who has previously attained knowledge of his own Self necessarily attains liberation (*kaivalya*); therefore, regarding the attainment of knowledge of one's own Self, there is no difference at the time of death whether there is recollection or non-recollection. Now, let there be no distinction for this knower of the Self between a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and a non-ford; however, as for that which [occurs] at the final moment...

Even regarding "one whose memory has failed": if, at the moment of the body's fall, there is a forgetting of that very knowledge of one's own self which was grasped as the means, then how could he be liberated? As it is said: "Even at the time of death, remembering Me alone, having cast off the body..."
"He who departs [with this thought] attains the state of being; there is no doubt about this" (Gītā 8.5).
Thus it is said in the Śrī Gītā. Even so, in this context, the utility belongs to remembrance alone;
page 162.

Even if it were the case that one attains the state of the Supreme Lord at the time of death even in the absence of remembrance of Him, then every common person, though deluded at the moment of death, would attain union with the Supreme Lord due to the lack of any distinction; furthermore, scriptural passages of this kind would become non-authoritative. This, however, is not the case.

And to this [objection], he gives the reply: "liberated at the same time as knowledge. It is true that there is no utility for him in memory; rather, at the very moment the true guru imparts the instruction regarding the knowledge of one's own Self as the Great Lord into his ear, at that very instant [he realizes]: "I alone am all this."

One who has ascended to the supreme reality of self-knowledge, whose state of being enveloped by the sheaths of māyā and the rest has dissolved, requires nothing else; carrying the body merely as a residual impression like the whirling of a potter’s wheel, he is no longer subject to the torment of remembering or not remembering it in subsequent time. For:
When there is a connection with the *kañcukas* of *āṇava* and *māyīya* born of ignorance, the bodily *kañcuka* comes into being.

Through the instruction of the knowledge of one's own Self, because of the destruction of the *kañcukas* born of ignorance, how could the bodily *kañcuka*, which is already as good as destroyed, ultimately cause any constraint for the Knower?
"Is it enough?"— at the very moment of explaining the knowledge of one's own self, he would become liberated while still alive.
As it is said in the *Sāhasrikā Kularatnamālikā*:
When the excellent teacher explains it correctly, then without doubt he is liberated at that very moment and remains merely like a machine.
Thus it is said; and in the venerable *Niśāṭana* as well:
"Whether for the duration of milking a cow or the flight of an arrow, one who is once joined to the supreme reality is liberated and shall liberate others."
Since he previously spent even a moment placing his self within Brahman,
how could he fail to remember it when the end of his life has arrived?

Thus it is said. Alternatively, by whom is the final moment of the knower of the Self experienced—experienced solely through its own self-awareness—by virtue of which its remembrance or non-remembrance might be postulated? To the extent that this is not within the range of those who see only the near side, the omniscient ones must be questioned regarding it; but certainly not [those of limited vision].

Even for one who has realized the ultimate truth at the time of death, the moment of casting off the body can be inferred as auspicious or inauspicious based solely on the movements of the body. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, who resides within one's own self, necessarily [manifests] for that knower of self-knowledge who is always permeated by that state.
At the time of death, he causes one to remember one's own true nature, even though it has become like wood or stone.
As it is said:
O Nārada, those mortals who, while in their normal state of activity, remember me—
I remember them at the time of death as being like wood or stone.
Likewise,
when the mind is steady and the body is perfectly healthy, and while the equilibrium of the bodily constituents remains established, that man who is possessed of wisdom beholds my universal form.
Then, when my devotee— who has become like a piece of wood or a stone— is dying, I remember him and lead him to the supreme goal.

Thus it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Lakṣmīsaṃhitā*. In this regard, the cause is precisely the state of being constantly permeated by that [object] (*tadbhāvabhāvitatvam*); otherwise, how could even a memory arise at the end in the absence of the firmness of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from prior experience? Thus, no one who possesses knowledge (*jñānin*) would have any utility [in practice] at the moment of death. || 83 ||

If, however, resorting to sacred fords and the like does not, in any way whatsoever, constitute an auxiliary factor according to the manner described above, then why is it resorted to by the learned?— to this he states the distinction of the subject matter:
Service at sacred fords leads to merit;
going to the home of a dog-cooker for one's end leads to hell.
But if there is no contact with the stain of merit or demerit, what is the use of that? || 86 ||
For those wise ones whose grasp of the body and so forth as the subject has not yet dissolved, and who lack such confidence in the contemplation of the knowledge of their own Self, there occurs—
whether they are performing the accumulation of merit through sacrifices, public works, and the like, or the accumulation of demerit— [the aforementioned consequence].

Service at sacred fords such as Prayāga and the act of choosing a holy site (*kṣetra*) at the time of death will certainly lead to merit and the attainment of the highest worlds; likewise, the same applies to the "course of death" in the abode of a *śvapaca*.
That is to say, the course of death—the attainment of demise—in a most sinful place characterized by the dwellings of *śvapākas* and the like.

Why would these [beings] not fall into hell, such as the Avīci and other hells? Because the grasping at the body as the subject of cognition still persists. Having experienced enjoyment according to the circumstances of their death, they are born again in auspicious or inauspicious bodies and die once more—thus it continues.
Those who, through an uninterrupted succession of births and deaths,
identify the body and so forth as the self would be of such a nature. But for one who...
Through the firmness of the reflective awareness of one’s own true nature, the conceit of being a limited subject such as the body and so forth has completely dissolved.

When the contact with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) whose nature consists of merit and demerit has ceased for that one whose essential nature is the sky of consciousness, what is there left for him? Thus he...

Since the resorting to sacred fords and the like belongs to those who partake in auspicious and inauspicious karma, therefore, for the pure Knower (jñānin), there is no utility in such service to sacred fords and so forth. As it is said in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*:
"Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the King; he who dwells here within your heart."
If you have no dispute with that, then do not go to the Ganges, nor to Gayā.
Thus: here, the very conceit of identifying the body with the self (*dehātmamānitā*) residing in the heart is Yama;

for those by whom this has been devoured after perceiving the nature of the Great Lord who is one's own full Self, how could there be for them this exertion of service to sacred bathing places and the like?—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). || 84 ||
But was it not already established previously—

that the Self, whose nature as the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* has been burnt away by knowledge, remains established in its own true nature after the fall of the body and does not produce the sprout of rebirth, just as a burnt seed does not produce a shoot?

If the dissolution of the bodily sheath occurs simultaneously with the manifestation of one's own innate knowledge, then let it not be established hereafter; as for that which... [page 167] ...furthermore,
One might object: "While the binding of the sheath consisting of the body and so forth still exists, how could he not be permeated by the properties inherent in it?
And being thus permeated, why would he not be a transmigrating being once dead?"—this objection is refuted by the phrase "having completely separated the husk from the grain."
The space between the husk and the grain of rice does not bring about for the grain an identity with that [space], even though it resides within it. || 85 ||
In the same way, consciousness here, having been separated from the veil of the sheaths through purification,
remains as one whose self is liberated, even while still persisting.
She becomes devoid of that touch. || 86 ||
That which is the casting of husk-particles into the interior of the husk-skin of a grain of rice that has been thoroughly separated and detached from its husk and bran—
page 168—

Furthermore, there is a re-arrangement in that very same place as before; it is like the insertion of a grain of rice between the husks. Although it remains capable of producing a sprout by virtue of its nature as rice, it does not establish a firm identity or close contact with them; rather, the husk and the rice remain distinct, like two iron rods.

While they remain so, they do not become occupied with the production of a single effect; in the same way, for the Knower, this consciousness or awareness is separated from the mass of coverings—the collection of *kañcukas* such as the *āṇavamala*—and [realizes]:
"I alone am the nature of the Great Lord of my own Self, existing at all times and in all places as the Soul of the Universe."

"I am throbbing"—this [consciousness] has been uplifted through the firm cultivation of the knowledge of one's own Self; "here," meaning while remaining for some time within this veil of sheaths (*kañcuka*) in the form of a body by way of the persistence of residual impressions, she, though situated there, becomes one whose self is liberated, whose bonds are destroyed, and who is devoid of contact with them. Of her—
The contact with the veil-like covering of the body and so forth is that coloring (uparāga) produced by the karmic impurity consisting of merit and demerit.

It is capable of producing the sprout of saṃsāra; being "devoid" (vivarjitā) means it is abandoned by that [ignorance]. Just as rice placed between husks becomes devoid of the capacity for the growth of a sprout—this is what is meant. It would thus be said: saṃsāra has ignorance as its cause; therein...
For the yogin whose sheath has been shattered by the fully arisen knowledge of his own Self, consciousness is no longer a cause of transmigratory existence,

due to the deficiency of the causal complex produced by ignorance; nor does this bondage of the bodily sheath persist for him through the force of residual impressions during the remaining course of life, as its root— ignorance— has been consumed by the fire of knowledge.

"By the manifestation of one's own innate nature, one is capable of cutting off the sprout of saṃsāra"—thus, the Knower, while still alive, is of the nature of the Fourth (turya) due to the absence of the body, and is of the nature of that which transcends the Fourth (turyātīta); in either case, there is no longer any suspicion of saṃsāra. || 86 ||

[The opponent objects: "But surely, as long as the yogin’s consciousness remains situated within the body by means of residual impressions—even though its own true nature has been realized—it must still be impure, because even a portion of the turbidity caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body continues to exist. [The author] refutes this with an analogy:
The state of stainlessness [of the jewel] within the container is fashioned by a most skillful artisan.
Even a soiled gem, when separated from its limiting adjuncts, has a nature that is essentially pure.
Thus, through the perception of the stainless state of the True Guru’s teaching,
even one who is liberated from the subtle adjunct is [freed] from other adjuncts.
The form of Śiva appears as if empty. || 88 ||
Just as a gem, though its purity has been brought forth by a highly skilled lapidary, appears dirty or even greyish when it is enclosed within a casket, yet that very same gem,
upon the removal of the condition of the casket and the absence of any particular covering, becomes clear in its ultimate nature exactly as it is.
He becomes one whose essential nature is stainless. In this very manner—
[page 171]—
this perception is the stainless state of the teaching of the true Guru.
That [state] belongs to one who has thus become such: a preeminent teacher possessing full knowledge of his own self;

through the thorough cultivation of his teaching—the method of instruction on the secret of self-knowledge—the persistence of the *āṇavamala*, which is of the nature of impurity and serves as the foundation for the *māyīya* and *kārmamala*, has been removed. It is of this kind.
Due to the destruction of the fundamental impurity (*mala*), even that perception which has the nature of space becomes liberated from the subtle adjunct— the "subtle" being the body,

and the "adjunct" being its defining characteristic; thus, being separated from it and due to the absence of any other limiting attributes, that very form of Śiva shines forth upon the dissolution of the body.

The meaning is that it shines as the state of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivatva*). Just as a gem shines in its own true nature when freed from the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a casket, in the same way, consciousness—which is inherently pure—shines as truly pure through the realization of its own nature upon the dissolution of the limiting adjunct of the body, which is considered impure. Now, one might object:

Just as a gem, even when freed from the limiting condition of its casket, becomes stained again by assuming some other limiting condition, so too consciousness, even though released from the limiting condition of the body, would become stained once more if it were to grasp another limiting condition, just like the gem.
"It is indeed impure because it possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),"— thus he refutes [the objection] with the words "even though it is devoid of other limiting adjuncts.
There is not an absolute similarity between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), since, after the fall of his body...

For that whose body is great light and whose nature is supreme non-duality, all this which is considered an adjunct shines as if it were its own limb; therefore, since there is no other distinct adjunct,
it is not further qualified by another adjunct— thus, there is no similarity with the apprehension of an adjunct by means of a gem.

Indeed, the assumption of the limiting adjuncts of the body has ignorance as its root; if that is shattered by the axe of knowledge of one's own Self, how could there ever again be recourse to such adjuncts? As it is said: "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded."
"But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun" (Gītā 3.16). Therefore, through the knowledge of one's own true nature, the yogi possesses self-awareness at all times.
It is indeed pure—thus [it is said]. || 88 ||
In the arising of all conditioned phenomena (*upādhi*),
the only cause is the growth of mental formations (*manasaḥ saṃskāra*) whose activity has been correctly cultivated; it is not, however, [any other].
"Something new is emerging"— this state of being absorbed in that [reality] is indicated by the authority of the scriptures and other sources,
even through unwavering faith.
He himself has previously attained heaven, hell, and the human state. || 89 ||
Whether through the authority of scripture (*āgama*), through the oral transmission of the lineage of teachers (*gurupadeśapāramparya*), through the cultivation of reasoning (*yukti*),

or through faith firmly rooted in prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding self-knowledge, a cognizer who has practiced either in the knowledge of one's own self or in the fettered rites of sacrifice and charity (*iṣṭāpūrta*) attains identification with that very state at that moment, through the growth of those latent impressions.

Having attained the very nature of each respective object with which he was habituated, after the fall of the body, he attains—according to the conformity of his latent impressions (vāsanā)—heaven, which is unsurpassed bliss; hell, which is the suffering of Avīci and other such states;
or the human condition, which consists of both pleasure and pain; and not otherwise.
Even for a person whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have not been cultivated,
[something] occurs simply upon the fall of the body; for every cognizer, by whatever disposition (*āśaya*), [acts].

Whatever one practices, one becomes of that very nature at that very time; however, at the moment of death, whatever object has been clearly desired manifests for the perceiver— thus, there can never be a reversal of the practiced object, nor can any unpracticed object appear as something entirely new.
The meaning is that in all cases, prior habit alone is the cause. || 89 ||

Thus, for one who knows their own self, being constantly permeated by that state [of consciousness] at the time of leaving the body is the cause for the full manifestation [of reality]; however, one should not imagine that some visible worldly occasion of death, consisting of merit or demerit, is the cause of heaven, hell, and so forth— thus he says:
But the final moment therein,
while sustaining a meritorious or sinful state,
acts as a cooperative cause for the deluded.
But when it has reached its state of existence, that [prior] cause is no longer the cause for its motion. || 90 ||
Even those such as beasts, birds, and reptiles who know their own course of existence as being of that very nature [attain it].
They too, being refined by their ancient awakening, go to that state. || 91 ||

Thus, when the possessor of knowledge has been established in this way, at the final moment— the last instant coinciding with the destruction of the body— he experiences, while being served by those perceivers standing nearby, a state that is either meritorious or sinful, inferred from their perception of his suffering due to a corrupted disease caused by an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

It becomes a cooperative cause, indeed a causal factor, only for those deluded perceivers who identify the body with the self. Let that wretched thing [the body] proceed as it may; nevertheless, for that yogin—who has shattered the identification of the body with the self and is ever adept at contemplating his own Self as the Great Lord—that final moment does not count toward [liberation].
It may be argued that [karma] is the cause or the reason for the transition from one body to another. To demonstrate how this [conclusion] follows, he says: "Even those who...
(page 176).

Thus, even those who— due to some particular intention, or by means of a curse and the like— have attained birth in a sinful womb or even the form of an animal, should recognize their own course (svagati), that is, their own state (ātmasthiti), as the Self at the time of death; for although they are deluded, they are favored by the awakening of the latent impressions of the knowledge of the Self practiced in previous lives.
And they attain the state of abiding in their own Self. Just as in the case of the liberation of the lordly elephant and others,
even though the elephant was by nature a mere beast, through the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of devotion to the Supreme Lord previously cultivated,
he praised the Blessed Viṣṇu and, having completely cast off his covering (*kañcuka*), realized his own true nature.

What was the cause for his recollection there? The meaning is this: due to the influence of humoral imbalances arising from the body and so forth, the Knower may abandon the body while acting like a piece of wood or a stone, muttering whatever comes to mind—be it merit, sin, or even the names of cats and such; yet, by this much, the knowledge and other qualities he had practiced while in a state of normal activity [are not lost].
There would be its total destruction; for the qualities residing in the body and so forth fall back only upon the body and so forth, and do not persist eternally—
as in the case of the expression "the monkey with the torch."
They are able to conceal a cultivated object; thus, until the moment of death, growth alone is the ultimate reality everywhere. As it is said in the Gītā:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one finally leaves the body,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, because one has been constantly absorbed in that. (8.6) Likewise:

"To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me" (10.10). Thus, it is precisely the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that serves as the cause for granting the ultimate goal. 91.

Thus, by means of this demonstrated vision, since the state of being constantly permeated by that [realization] has been established, nothing new whatsoever shall befall the knower at the destruction of the body, as it is viewed in its novelty; for it is shown that the body alone is perishable— it is merely the body that perishes, but not the sprouting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
