This person, situated within the interior of the body,
upon its dissolution, attains union with another body according to his own fitness.
Thus, at the moment of realization,
one's own self appears to him exactly as it is;
at that time, he is precisely such.
It does not become otherwise upon the fall of the body. || 93 ||

Therefore, the person (puruṣa) residing in the body, the jar, and so forth—the self (ātman) of everyone, permeated by the impurity of karma (kārmamala), whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is perfumed by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the fruits of actions performed with the intention of attaining heaven and the like—is "consisting of heaven" (svargamaya); because it is characterized by the fully developed latent impressions of the fruit of heaven, it is the enjoyer of the fruit of heaven. Thus [it is said].
...up to this point: thus, one who has been nurtured by the latencies of previously committed evil karma is the experiencer of the fruit of hell;

the body is merely the locus for experiencing the fruits of both types of karma, and upon its destruction, [the self remains] according to its own nature. Regarding that dissolution of the body, as it is for one's own self—
In accordance with its latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it immediately enters into a connection with another body as a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) by means of another [form of] existence,
through which [it continues] at a later time.
One becomes a partaker of the enjoyment of the fruits bestowed by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of specific past actions. In the same way, at the occasion of knowledge—

when the disciple's own self is being revealed by the Guru— his own self, which is consciousness (*caitanya*), manifests exactly as it is, once and for all, according to the sequence of the instruction.

Having reached the state of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by perfect sovereignty— whether limited or otherwise— he remains eternally such that his own self, as it was constantly reflected upon by the knower through its very own nature,
manifests to him in that same form due to the growth of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it does not manifest [differently] even at the fall of the body.

The self of the knower is otherwise veiled; for what has appeared cannot be unappeared, otherwise no one would practice anything at all, and thus there would be the total destruction of all worldly activity. By dharma there is upward movement, and by adharma there is downward movement.
Liberation results from knowledge, while bondage is held to arise from its opposite.
All such [arguments] would be rendered inconsistent; therefore, at the time of death, let the body be as it may—
indeed, let it be whatever it is— for the mere sprouting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) resides within one's own self for everyone.
The cause of both bondage and liberation—thus [it is said]. || 93 ||

If, however, the sensation of the pain of death should arise in the body due to an imbalance of the elements, this does not cause any hindrance to the growth of practice; thus, one strives to realize the very state that has been explained.
The confusion of the group of organs, loss of mindfulness, turbidity of the breath, its cessation,
and specific pains in the vital points.
Experience arises from the refinement of the body. || 94 ||
How could that knower not be [liberated] even when in a state of delusion at the time of death, given that he is already free from the conjunction of the body?
One does not fall away from the ultimate reality of one's own self. || 95 ||
The complete sublation of the group of thirteen instruments, both external and internal—
that is,
the total disappearance of their own nature— just as in the case of the sense organs such as the eyes and so forth.

They are not capable of perceiving objects such as form; likewise, the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, do not engage in speaking, grasping, and so forth; nor does the intellect determine the object according to its true nature;
the mind lacks stability; and even the ego-sense remains only intermittently in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus:

The loss of memory (*smṛtināśa*) is the total disappearance of an experienced object; even when entreated by his kinsmen, one on the verge of death does not recognize an object standing before him, though it has been experienced hundreds of times. Therefore, apart from being constantly permeated by that state [of consciousness], there is no other means—such as the teaching of the knowledge of Brahman or gifts at the time of death—to ensure this.
In that state, nothing whatsoever sprouts in the mind, like a painting in the sky;

rather, there is only the injunction: "This must be done," which is merely the sense of what ought to be performed. Likewise, there is the breath—the air in the throat—and its turbidity in the region of the throat, such as stammering or hiccupping. Furthermore, there is the piercing of the vital points (*marmans*).
In the joints of the bones there is a cracking sound; likewise,
there are specific types of pain, such as fever, diarrhea, and so forth— thus [is described] that which belongs to the body.

The experience arising from the bodily refinement—namely, the experience of suffering born of the body due to the imbalance of the elements of wind, bile, and phlegm within the sheath of the gross elements (bhūtakañcuka)—how could it not occur even for a knower when there is the conjunction with a physical form? It would certainly occur. For that reason, the knower always holds the conceit of the body and so forth beneath his feet.

And one who has entered into the state of his own Self as Maheśvara does not fall away from, nor undergo any alteration in, the true nature of the reflective awareness of consciousness that has taken root in the ultimate reality of his own Self, even when there is a connection with the bodily ignorance produced at the moment of death.

Since that knower has cast off the connection with the body, he cannot be made identical with it by the experience arising from it; yet, if— like an ordinary person— he does not perceive for even a moment immediately after the fall of the body,
then by this much, through his own intended purpose and his state of composed activity, that man of tranquil heart [attains his goal].
For one who has practiced devotion to the Lord, nothing unprecedented ever occurs;
therefore, the man of knowledge (jñānī) is liberated immediately upon the manifestation of his own Self, and not otherwise.

It has been established hundreds of times previously that the refinement of the body is a cause of bondage. How, then, can one who always identifies with the body and is composed of merit and demerit avoid becoming absorbed in it through the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which arise from the refinement of the body?
As it has been said:
"But when the embodied soul meets its end while sattva is predominant, then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Highest. (14.14)
And so forth. Qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are attributes of *prakṛti*; they exercise their constraint only upon one who is composed of them.

However, for one who has cultivated [the self] through its separation from them, these qualities are nothing at all—such is the entirely different path of the Knower (*jñānin*). On the other hand, those limited subjects (*paśu-pramātāraḥ*) who have not beheld the feet of a Guru [attribute] the qualities inherent in themselves [to the Self].

They attribute it otherwise, thinking: "If this one were truly wise, why would he eat and dress while his body is afflicted by disease and the like? Or, if he has fallen into a state of dullness at the time of death, why did he not remember anything?"—in this manner they judge.
Since they are afflicted by ignorance and thus dispute in many ways, by whom should they be questioned?
If this person were truly a knower (*jñānin*), yet he were still possessed of the bodily attributes and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), what would follow from that?

How could that be corrupted? For the wise one, even though the manifestation of his own self (*svātmaprakāśa*) appears diverse according to various states, it remains the manifestation of his own self alone; there is no loss of its nature as the experiencer of his own self, by which the knowledge would perish. Even Lord Vāsudeva possesses the greatness of the six perfections in their entirety.

In his incarnation as Kṛṣṇa, [the Lord] abandoned his physical body while experiencing pain caused by the strike of a hunter's arrow—having done this, did that Lord of the World suffer any loss of his own true nature? In this regard, the refinement of the body for everyone from a worm up to Sadāśiva is exactly like this; however, there is one difference.

The body is supported solely by the self-reflection of one's own nature, whereas the other possesses the false reality of identifying the body and so forth as the Self—this is the distinction. Therefore, the physical attributes of the knower and the ignorant are indeed identical;
yet, there is no equality of results on this account, as has been stated in the *Gītā*.
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature;
beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish? (3.33)
Thus [ends the verse]. 95.

Now, demonstrating that the cause is indeed the diverse descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*)— whether through non-sequential or sequential cultivation of the yoga of knowledge— he states the distinction of the results regarding this path of ultimate reality:
"This path of ultimate reality..."
When [the truth] comes instantly from the mouth of the Guru due to an extremely intense descent of power (śaktipāta),
then and there one becomes Śiva, free from all obstacles.

At whatever time a person of their final birth approaches—that is, fully attains—this path of the ultimate reality, which has been explained hundreds of times from the mouth of the Guru, the face of the preeminent teacher; this path characterized by perfect sovereignty, the secret route of the oral tradition consisting of self-awakening; whoever such a person is, he...
At that very moment, at that very occasion, immediately following the teacher’s instruction, having removed all obstacles, one shall become Śiva himself. As it is said in the *Śrīkula*:
O Dear One, whether by chance, in play, or even out of respect, he who possesses knowledge of reality is liberated at that very moment upon whose eyes he casts his gaze.
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: "How can such a secret oral tradition (mukhāmnāya) be imparted? To this he replies:

"By the descent of an exceedingly intense power" (*atitīvraśaktipātāt*). This refers to the descent—meaning the entry into the heart-lotus of the bound soul (*paśu*)—of that supreme Lord’s power known as Grace (*anugraha*), which is exceedingly intense and piercing, by means of which even a bound soul [is liberated].

Through the experience of the Guru’s grace, one becomes Śiva; that is to say, one is liberated even while living—just as the substance of copper becomes gold through the application of the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*). The meaning is this: the attainment of the knowledge of one's own Self is indeed the means of the Supreme Lord’s grace; therefore, it does not arise here from the power of necessity (*niyatiśakti*).

Rituals such as recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and sacrifice proceed by way of being means (*upāya*). However, for one whose heart has been pierced by the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*), the secret of the tradition concerning the face of the deity forcibly and instantaneously captivates the heart; thereby, one immediately attains the state of the Supreme Goddess. Thus, the sovereign power of the Supreme Lord is manifold and beyond questioning.
The descent of power (śaktipāta)—thus [it is said]. || 96 ||
Furthermore, for one whose descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred through the distinctions of medium, weak, or very weak intensity, that person,
reflecting upon the sequence of yoga by means of the Guru’s instruction until the moment of death, [attains liberation] upon the fall of the body (piṇḍapāta).
He demonstrates that the state of Śiva is attained by one who relies upon the form transcending all [levels] through the sequential order of the steps of the ladder.
Upon attaining the final ascent into the supreme reality, there is the state of being identical with Śiva.

Thus, indeed, due to the weakness of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), by not obtaining the instruction on complete knowledge, one resorts to and directly realizes the form that transcends all [levels], whose nature extends to the limit of all the *tattvas*. How? He says: "by the sequence of steps of the ladder. [The locations are] the *kanda*, the navel—

The steps consisting of the heart, throat, *lambikā*, *bindu*, *nāda*, and *śakti* are indeed the sacred sites (*tīrthas*) for ascending upwards; their "attainment" (*padam āsādanam*) is the process of gradual withdrawal and non-grasping, proceeding step by step from the *kanda*, then to the navel, and then to the heart— by means of such an ascent.
Thus, up until the attainment of the sprout of ultimate reality—
on the occasion of the attainment of the sprout of ultimate reality— the alms-round of that yogin proceeds gradually.
The state of abiding has the nature of Śiva; thus, this sequential method has been explained. || 97 ||

Even for a yogi who practices the yoga of gradual stages and has attained composure, such an ascension may not occur, and obstacles to the attainment of the desired goal may arise; if death were to occur before the ultimate reality has been realized, what would happen? He [the author] dispels this doubt as follows:
But for him who has not yet reached the stream consisting of the ultimate reality and rests in the middle state,
there is a longing for the attainment of that state.
The death of the mind might also sometimes occur. || 98 ||
He is described in the scripture as one who has fallen from yoga, yet he is the lord of a world of manifold enjoyments by virtue of his place of rest.
Having been so, one becomes Śiva in another birth. || 99 ||
Thus, for one practicing yoga through the method of leaping (*ullaṅghana-krama*), due to some obstacle,
there may be a resting in the middle; because experience is then perceived even in some particular *cakra* or *ādhāra*, one finds complete satisfaction right there.

Of one who has departed from this very state and thus has not reached the stream consisting of the ultimate reality— the state of the supreme principle (paratattva) which was promised and transcends all paths— or rather,
of one whose mind is eager to attain that state and who still possesses the longing to achieve the promised existence of the ultimate reality.

If, at some point, a misfortune is anticipated in the midst of practice, then what is the fate of this person who has not yet attained the gain [of realization] from his alms-gathering? To this he says: "fallen from yoga," and so forth. He is said—that is, declared—in the *śāstra*, the scriptural treatise, to have fallen or deviated from yoga, that is, from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), in both ways. Of what nature would he be?

To this he says, "Variegated," and so forth. From the very act of casting off the body (*piṇḍapāta*), there are variegated enjoyments—worlds consisting primarily of various wonders such as women, food, drink, garlands, garments, ointments, song, and instrumental music—which are conducive to one's own repose and are the abodes of the Lords of the *tattvas*. In those [worlds], he is the Lord (*pati*).
Immediately upon death, one is endowed with divine enjoyments— this is the meaning.
Upon the exhaustion of the authority over those enjoyments—
[page 190] —
Furthermore, how might that one who has fallen from yoga [attain success] again? To this he says: "By resting," and so forth.

By virtue of the location of the resting place—such as the *kanda* (the bulbous root)—and through the power of awakening the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that practice, he [attains it] in another birth, namely, in a second life.

Having become [such a one] in saṃsāra, having obtained a body qualified for the practice of yoga, and having undertaken with effort the yoga previously practiced, he effortlessly ascends to the state consisting of the supreme reality as promised in a prior birth; upon the falling away of the body, he becomes Śiva himself. || 99 ||

Now, for the yogin who, despite practicing yoga, fails to attain even the slightest rest in any single point due to mental instability, yet remains possessed of faith toward yoga— what might be his state after the fall of the body? To this, he says:
For by practicing this path of ultimate truth, even if one has not yet attained yoga,
one becomes a partaker of the enjoyments of the celestial realms.
With a joyful mind, one rejoices for a very long time. || 100 ||
Just as a sovereign emperor is honored by all people within his realm, so too is he honored by all beings regarding sense objects.
Thus, one who has fallen from yoga is always to be honored by all the gods in the worlds. || 101 ||

If, even after practicing this path— the true nature of self-knowledge which has been explained hundreds of times— and serving it with faith and devotion, one fails to attain the rest characterized by yoga as it truly is due to the instability of mental defects, and dies while still in the midst of this life;
Then that one fallen from yoga,
by the power of the grace of faith and devotion rooted in the subject matter of the yoga of knowledge,
becomes a partaker of the enjoyments of the world of the gods; with a joyful heart, he experiences delight for a very long time, even along with the gods.

He becomes worthy of worship in the worlds, each in its own respective place. To the question "Like what?", he says: "The universal monarch," and so forth. Just as a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*), a sovereign ruler of the seven continents, is worshipped and honored by all people throughout the various realms and territories, even so is this one.
One whose sphere of merit and demerit has been exhausted,
who has attained dispassion, and who is in his final birth— he is worthy of our veneration, for [he has realized] it within his own self.
"In a previous birth, there was an effort for the sake of inquiry"—this is what is being praised even by the gods; such is the meaning. || 100 ||
What happens immediately after his cessation of authority over enjoyment in other worlds? To this he says:
"Having regained human status after a long time, and having practiced yoga."
One attains divine immortality, from which one does not return again. || 102 ||
Having enjoyed the pleasures in the celestial worlds as previously described, after a very long time, that one who has fallen from yoga returns to the human state in this cycle of existence;
having obtained a body fit for the practice and means of yoga, [he does so] because of the mental restlessness in his previous birth.

That very yoga which had become difficult to attain was reached through the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of yogic tendencies firmly rooted by devotion and faith born in previous lives; thus,
in this very final birth, there is the attainment of liberation, ending the bondage of future births.
The meaning is as follows:
having attained and thoroughly practiced [this] without effort, one attains divine immortality at the end of the body.
One perceives the essential nature of the supreme reality (paratattva) and attains firmness in that supreme nature—this is the meaning.

For this very reason, there can be no returning for him from that state. Thus, even the slightest reflection upon the great auspiciousness of the subject matter of self-knowledge does not lead to the path of transmigratory existence.
As it is said in the Śrī Gītā:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear" (2.40).
Thus: "Likewise,
one who lacks self-restraint, though endowed with faith, and whose mind has wavered from yoga, having failed to attain perfection in yoga— " (6.37).
Starting from the question beginning with these words, [it continues]:
"One who has been perfected through many births then attains the supreme goal" (7.45).
Thus, even though the entire section ending with the latter [verse] has been expounded by the Sage, it should be kept in mind—so [it is said]. || 102 ||

Thus, for a living being who has been touched even slightly by this sequence of the yoga of knowledge, there arises such an excellence of power that it cannot be described; therefore, those whose hearts are moistened by discernment should, with their whole being, remain vigilant toward the cessation of birth and death— this is what he establishes.
Therefore, whoever is devoted to this true path attains the state of Śiva;
having realized this in the ultimate truth—
Nevertheless, one must strive in whatever way possible. || 103 ||
Since the practice of self-reflection (*svātmapratyavamarśa*) leads to the attainment of the supreme fruit through the sequence thus established, therefore, in this regard—
[page 195] —
On this most beautiful path, which leads to supreme liberation, it is shown that there is no restriction regarding eligibility by stating "whosoever is devoted. Any person whatsoever,
being tormented by hundreds of afflictions such as birth, death, and disease, who is completely devoted through the intellect of discrimination—

"Delighting"—having become full of faith in that very [teaching] and being immersed in it—that living being, having shaken off all the afflictions of saṃsāra, attains the state of Śiva; that is, he reaches the condition which is the supreme good in a single lifetime itself, in a short time. As it is said in the scripture, the *Śivadharmottara*:
Let this liberation in a single lifetime first be examined;
by whom can liberation over many lifetimes be prevented for you?

Thus, having reflected and deliberated in this manner, one should strive—that is, exert oneself with great effort—in that ultimate reality by whatever means possible. Considering that effort directed toward the primary goal is fruitful, one should not entertain even the slightest negligence regarding this matter; for by such practice of yoga—
If the firm rooting of one's own self has arisen, our desired goal is accomplished; if not, then the attainment of another divine world [is the result]. Even from that...

For one who has returned [to worldly life], there is once again a connection with yoga by virtue of the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of yoga previously practiced; thus, through the cultivation of the path to the highest good, nothing adverse befalls the practitioner.
Therefore, not even the slightest pride should be entertained regarding the means for achieving the supreme human goal.
Auspiciousness. || 103 ||

Thus, having established the instruction on the *Paramārthasāra* as taught by the venerable Śeṣa, according to the sequence of the non-dual teaching of Śiva and supported by reasoning, experience, and scripture, the author of this treatise— seeking only his own personal satisfaction— first reveals his own name and states that this indeed is the instruction.
Describing this as the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), he states the conclusion of the book’s meaning:
"For one who meditates upon this summary of the Supreme Brahman uttered by Abhinavagupta..."
Before long, one attains the state of Śiva and the penetration of one's own heart. || 104 ||

This has been set forth at length to establish that for one who meditates upon the supreme, most excellent Brahman— the very nature of one's own self, which consists of perfect bliss because it causes all things to expand— [liberation] is attained without effort.

For a person who reflects upon their own self, [liberation] occurs before long—that is, very quickly—and not, however, only at the end of many births. Thus, for one who has become Brahman in this manner, the state of Śiva is attained;
the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) becomes possible. How? By effecting the entry of the Self into one's own heart, [one realizes] the Self...

Having entered the heart, which is the locus of reflective awareness—what kind of Brahman is that? It is such that its "compendium," meaning its essential purport, has been uttered and revealed by Abhinavagupta, whose name is to be celebrated.
And here, under the pretext of his name, this may also be said: he who is "Abhinava" (the New) [is distinct] from others...

The supreme secret of the Brahman remained unseen, hidden, and as if concealed; such was that which arose and was revealed in this concise form—that is, the Brahman of this nature. By communicating it in this way, the rarity of the instruction has been established.
It may be so. || 104 ||

Determining the extent of the work, the author states the authorship of this treatise: "This essence of the scriptures, which is exceedingly profound, has been condensed here in one hundred Āryā verses."
By me, Abhinavagupta, illuminated by the remembrance of the feet of Śiva. || 105 ||

This essence of the treatises—that most excellent reality (*satattva*) which exists within many books—could not be established even by thousands of volumes; yet, having accepted that very same [reality], I have expressed it in a brief work consisting of one hundred verses. By this, his skill in creative intuition (*pratibhākauśala*) is demonstrated.

By what kind of self? "Illumined by the remembrance of Śiva’s feet. Of Śiva—who is the nature of supreme bliss, who abides in one's own self, and whose sole form is consciousness-bliss—those "feet" are the rays of consciousness;
their "remembrance" is the constant contemplation at every moment during the perception of objects such as sound.

It is the non-forgetting of one's own experience; by that, it is "blazing," radiant with the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*). For this very reason, its name is to be celebrated. Otherwise, how could one who identifies the self with the body and so forth know their own true Self?
Is the status of being the author and the qualified authority for this extensive teaching on the great purpose (mahārtha) of the true reality of Maheśvara tenable?

For it is said that whatever is of a certain nature is capable of discerning that very nature; thus, by this statement, the teacher must be declared to possess the nature of Maheśvara who has entered [into the disciple]. May there be auspiciousness! 105.
Thus ends the *Paramārthasāra*, composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
By me, the disciple of that Śrīmat Kṣemarāja—who possesses the oral tradition of the true guru and has directly realized the Great Lord (Maheśa). (1)
This commentary, named *Yoga*, which consists of the full non-duality, has been composed by the ascetic Virakta, whose abode is the city of Śrī Vitastā. || 2 ||
This *Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti* is complete; it is the work of the venerable and supreme devotee of Maheśvara, the illustrious Rājānaka Yogarāja.
